changes.change: Add a small secure monotonic event counter and tamper-evident status element to the next pendant revision, exposed to the relay as part of every physical interaction and privacy/approval state transition. The counter must survive power loss and the status element must make 'capturing', 'playing', 'latched', and 'awaiting approval' distinguishable without relying on the single shared LED timing language.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The owner would be able to trust that a physical press or privacy state was neither replayed nor silently lost, and could tell the pendant's security state at a glance even when the Mac and relay are unreachable.
changes.effort: High: hardware revision plus secure nonvolatile counter integration, firmware protocol changes, relay verification, and usability testing in daylight and at night.
changes.risk: A failed counter or indicator could block legitimate interactions. Fail closed for approvals and privacy transitions, but retain a recovery path through a deliberate local reset that does not erase the audit epoch.
changes.cost_impact: Roughly a few dollars in components and board-layout cost; negligible steady-state power, with occasional nonvolatile writes requiring wear-leveling.
changes.latency_impact: Adds only a few milliseconds to local state transitions and negligible radio payload overhead.
changes.security_impact: Strengthens replay resistance and makes security state observable locally. It does not replace the existing physical approval or privacy-latch semantics.
depends_on: A defined signed event-envelope protocol
Relay-side monotonic-counter validation and rollback handling
A hardware design with an additional indicator channel and protected nonvolatile storage

changes.change: Install a fail-closed 'blind-spot contract' between perception, judgement, and speech. Every answer that implies absence ('nothing waiting', 'calendar is clear', 'all done') must carry source-readability evidence and a freshness bound. If a permission, browser session, relay, or device feed is unreadable, the system must say what it could not inspect, suppress the all-clear claim, and offer a bounded fallback. Make this a shared enforcement point used by notifications, day-plan, briefings, catchup, and pendant speech—not another triage module.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The owner should be able to trust a quiet answer. Today an unauthorised EventKit read can look exactly like an empty calendar, and several speech paths have no confidentiality or uncertainty gate. This change prevents reassuring fiction and tells the owner precisely what remains unknown.
changes.effort: Medium: define a small typed evidence contract, thread it through existing readers and speech entry points, add regression cases for denied permissions/offline browser/stale relay, and expose a compact spoken/dashboard explanation.
changes.risk: Initially produces more 'I could not check that' responses and may surface false positives if freshness thresholds are wrong. Recover by keeping the old result internally, making the contract inspectable, and allowing an owner-set freshness policy; never downgrade unreadable to empty.
changes.cost_impact: Negligible runtime cost; one deterministic validation per answer. A short fallback explanation may add a few realtime tokens only when a source is unavailable.
changes.latency_impact: Under 10 ms for local validation; unavailable-source fallbacks should not wait on retries unless explicitly requested.
changes.security_impact: Improves privacy by preventing sensitive fallback content from being spoken and makes source provenance explicit. It must not turn sensitivity labels into access permissions.
depends_on: A shared source-readability/freshness result from Mac and browser adapters
Threading evidence references through briefing, day-plan, notification, and pendantSpeech paths
Owner-editable freshness and disclosure policy with conservative defaults

changes.change: Add a delivery-aware release controller for important audio. Before enqueueing, it attaches one stable artifact/brief-item ID; after generation it waits for a bounded pendant delivery window. On no_audio, checksum_error, repeated interruption, or stale device ACK, it stops retrying blindly, invokes cross-surface preflight, and offers the owner a short Mac-speaker fallback or leaves the item in the durable pendant inbox. A single receipt records the exact branch and never counts server generation as owner delivery.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: Important information will not silently disappear just because the server succeeded. The owner gets one honest fallback instead of duplicate speech, endless retries, or a false 'done.'
changes.effort: Medium: join IDs across the relay/Mac pipeline, add a small release state machine, and wire the existing ACK/event and Mac audio actions.
changes.risk: A transient LTE outage could delay a briefing or cause an unwanted Mac fallback. Recover with a conservative timeout, owner-visible 'queued/not heard' state, idempotency key, and explicit disable switch; never auto-send the same audio twice.
changes.cost_impact: Negligible API cost; one small state record and existing event writes. Mac fallback uses local TTS/audio resources.
changes.latency_impact: Adds up to the configured delivery wait for important items; ordinary low-priority items remain queue-only.
changes.security_impact: Fallback must pass the same spoken-content redaction policy as pendant audio. Do not expose raw error payloads or private briefing text in relay logs.
depends_on: A durable relay-job/Mac-job/artifact join (currently only telemetry localJobId exists)
The accepted audio_delivery_ack_queue firmware behavior
A policy value defining which items are important enough to wait or fall back
A safe Mac audio executor path

changes.change: Add a small secure element with a protected device key, monotonic counter, and tamper-evident pairing state to the pendant; use it to sign physical approvals, host-pairing changes, privacy-latch transitions, and delivery receipts. Keep content and transcripts out of the secure element.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can know that an approval or revocation really came from the device in their hand, even if a Mac session, browser extension, or relay credential is stale or compromised. This makes the pendant a trustworthy personal key rather than merely a microphone and speaker.
changes.effort: Moderate hardware revision and firmware/relay protocol work; requires key provisioning, recovery design, and migration from current software-only signing.
changes.risk: Lost or damaged pendant could strand the owner's trust boundary; provide a second-device or in-person recovery ceremony, never a voice-only bypass. Counter wear and provisioning mistakes require manufacturing tests and a rollback-safe epoch scheme.
changes.cost_impact: Roughly $1–$4 BOM increase and negligible steady-state power; engineering and secure provisioning are the substantial costs.
changes.latency_impact: A few milliseconds per signature; no noticeable conversational delay if signatures are attached to existing envelopes.
changes.security_impact: Strongly improves non-repudiation and revocation. It does not protect content after a legitimate host is authorized, so least-privilege scopes and relay-side expiry remain required.
depends_on: A durable device identity and host-pairing protocol
physical_transaction_approval_latch semantics
relay-side revocation epochs
A recovery ceremony that does not rely on the same Mac session being revoked

changes.change: Add a compact, provenance-linked outcome event whenever the owner accepts, rejects, corrects, cancels, or undoes an agent action; store only action class, policy version, surface, result, and receipt IDs, then project aggregate counts into the weekly autonomy report.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The system can finally learn from the owner's actual corrections instead of repeating the same annoying behavior, without retaining the private content of the task.
changes.effort: Medium: extend the existing action ledger/receipt path, add a durable event writer, and expose a read-only aggregate route.
changes.risk: A mistaken inference could bias future autonomy. Keep events advisory, require explicit policy approval for changes, and allow deletion by event ID; recover by rebuilding aggregates from receipts.
changes.cost_impact: Negligible storage and model cost; weekly aggregation is background work.
changes.latency_impact: No added latency to action execution if events append asynchronously.
changes.security_impact: Metadata-only by default; redact targets and never store page/mail bodies. Provenance IDs remain local and revocable.
depends_on: A durable relay-job/Mac-job join
An owner-visible policy diff and approval path

changes.change: Create one durable briefing manifest mapping each spoken item to an opaque audio artifact, evidence references, and delivery state; have the relay fold record_pendant_delivery_event into it and expose only missing-item state to the owner.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The pendant stops pretending a server-completed job was heard, and the owner can recover exactly what was missed after a link drop or interruption.
changes.effort: Medium-high: schema and idempotency work across relay, pipeline, and pendant ACK ingestion.
changes.risk: Out-of-order or replayed device events could mark an item incorrectly. Enforce authenticated device sessions, monotonic sequence checks, eventId deduplication, and an append-only audit trail.
changes.cost_impact: Small D1/storage increase; audio generation cost falls because finished items are never regenerated.
changes.latency_impact: Sub-second state updates after delivery ACK; no impact on normal playback.
changes.security_impact: Opaque IDs only; no spoken content in ACKs. Respect privacy-panic revocation epochs.
depends_on: Wire audio_delivery_ack_queue firmware behavior to the live relay
A durable item/artifact manifest

changes.change: Add a press-to-start private rehearsal mode: the Mac assembles a time-bounded source bundle from the next calendar event and currently open browser tabs, the relay creates one cited 60-second audio item, and the pendant asks exactly one follow-up question before revealing any sensitive detail.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: Meeting preparation becomes a useful hands-free conversation rather than another long briefing, while the owner retains a physical boundary before private names or document details are spoken.
changes.effort: High: meeting lookup, browser source bounding, source-linked synthesis, and a pendant state machine for one-question interaction.
changes.risk: Wrong event or stale tab context could mislead the owner. Require explicit event/source IDs, freshness checks, a preflight, and a visible draft before audio; never mutate external systems.
changes.cost_impact: About $0.05–$0.20 per preparation, mostly synthesis and document extraction.
changes.latency_impact: 15–30 seconds to prepare; conversational follow-up under 1.5 seconds.
changes.security_impact: Sensitive content stays local until physical press; source snippets are redacted and expire. No mail/calendar writes.
depends_on: An event lookup surface with readable permission provenance
Bounded read-only browser extraction
A private spoken-content policy and pendant physical approval

changes.change: Build a content-independent provenance and deletion graph: every persisted derivative receives a source capsule/capture/audio/job edge, and a confirmed forget operation traverses those edges across Mac, browser, relay, and pendant, returning signed per-surface deletion acknowledgements.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: When the owner deletes something, it would actually be gone everywhere the system copied or inferred it from, with an honest proof of which surfaces succeeded or remain offline.
changes.effort: Very high: add provenance edges to existing records, migrate stores, implement idempotent tombstone propagation, and handle offline acknowledgements.
changes.risk: Over-broad traversal could delete unrelated material. Require a preview, exact source scope, physical confirmation, per-edge authorization, and an undo window only for tombstones—not recovered content.
changes.cost_impact: Moderate storage and engineering cost; negligible per-request inference cost.
changes.latency_impact: Local preview is fast; remote completion may wait for disconnected browser, relay, or pendant surfaces.
changes.security_impact: Strongly improves privacy, but deletion receipts and graph edges can themselves reveal relationships; retain only opaque IDs and sensitivity-minimized metadata.
depends_on: A durable cross-surface ID join
A universal privacy deletion policy
Relay and pendant acknowledgement handling

changes.change: Install a closed-loop spoken-audio quality controller that consumes authenticated pendant delivery ACKs and UART-derived metrics, maintains a per-session health state, and emits a signed profile decision (hold, retry once, lower complexity, or defer) at the next utterance boundary. Persist the decision and its evidence beside the pipeline receipt, and require a matching pendant ACK before marking an utterance delivered.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The owner stops hearing clipped, late, or missing answers without being told what happened; when quality is genuinely poor, the system degrades deliberately and preserves the current brief item instead of talking over failure.
changes.effort: Medium-high: relay state machine, firmware profile ACK/status frame, and Mac pipeline adapter; reuse existing event and receipt schemas where possible.
changes.risk: A bad controller could lower quality unnecessarily or loop retries. Bound retries, keep a known-good profile, require hysteresis, and expose a one-tap rollback/diagnostic draft. If telemetry is missing, queue rather than claim success.
changes.cost_impact: Negligible runtime/API cost; modest D1 telemetry growth capped by per-session retention. Firmware change is engineering cost, not a new hardware bill.
changes.latency_impact: At most one utterance-boundary decision; normal playback is unchanged. Failure detection adds 1–5 seconds of telemetry lag.
changes.security_impact: Opaque authenticated IDs only; no transcript in telemetry. Signed profile commands and monotonic device sequence numbers prevent stale or forged quality decisions.
depends_on: The accepted audio_delivery_ack_queue must emit authenticated playback events.
The accepted pendant_diagnostics_and_bug_draft parser must expose normalized metrics to the relay.
A typed audio-profile apply/rollback route must be implemented; current pipeline inspection alone cannot change the profile.

changes.change: Make browser target identity mandatory at the bridge boundary: browser_list_tabs returns a signed target token containing tabId, origin, title digest, and session ID; every read/click/type carries that token; browser result handling rejects any response whose tabId/session/origin differs, and stale default-session fallback is removed. On mismatch, return candidates without page content and require a fresh target selection.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The owner will stop getting answers or actions from the wrong browser tab—especially dangerous when YouTube, dashboards, and authenticated sites coexist. Ambiguity becomes an audible question instead of a silent leak or mistaken click.
changes.effort: Medium: bridge protocol and extension result schema, plus regression tests for stale-session override and tab closure/navigation. No model training required.
changes.risk: Some existing browser jobs will fail closed until they supply the token; recover by re-listing tabs and rebinding. A tab navigation can legitimately change title/URL, so compare origin and session plus a navigation generation rather than exact title alone.
changes.cost_impact: Negligible runtime/API cost; a few hundred bytes of metadata per command.
changes.latency_impact: Adds one deterministic verification (<50 ms locally) and may add one tab-list round on mismatch.
changes.security_impact: Substantially reduces cross-tab authenticated disclosure and wrong-target mutation. Target tokens must be opaque, short-lived, and never contain page text or credentials.
depends_on: A browser extension change to echo authoritative tab/session identity in every result
A durable command target token and result validator
Existing browser command lease sweep must be started so stale commands cannot linger

changes.change: Add a real wear/presence channel to the next pendant revision: a low-power skin-contact or capacitive sensor with a debounced, signed worn/unworn state and a short local transition history. The relay must treat unworn as a hard boundary for private audio and owner confirmation, while the Mac can continue non-private work. Do not infer wearing from Bluetooth/LTE reachability or button activity.
changes.why_useful_to_owner: The system could finally know whether speech is going to the owner’s ear or sitting on a desk in front of other people. Private briefings, approvals, and interruption decisions could fail closed instead of guessing from idle time or an absent link.

denied.scope: macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions for AI Pendant Agent, plus reconnect/authorize the AI Pendant Browser Bridge extension
denied.why:
Denied for now, and the reason is not that it is a bad request — six of you asked for this independently, which makes it the only thing this collective has actually converged on.

It cannot be granted from inside this harness. macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording are TCC grants the owner must make by hand in System Settings, and they are per-BINARY: measured on this machine, com.aipendant.agent (~/Applications/AI Pendant Agent.app) is trusted for input while com.anthropic.claudefordesktop failed the same probe in the same second. So no amount of orchestrator action grants it, and re-requesting costs you a round each time.

Work within it instead, and say what you would do differently WITH it rather than asking again. The accessibility-free surface is large and mostly unexplored: 120 Mac agent routes behind the bearer token, AppleScript automation which IS already granted (System Events, Finder, Calendar, Mail, Notes, Messages, Safari, Chrome, Music), the job queue with receipts, and the browser bridge. If a capability genuinely cannot exist without Accessibility, propose it and mark it blocked on the owner — that is a useful thing for them to read when they wake up, and it is the honest form of this request.

Re-request only if the owner grants it and the probe changes.
denied.risk: Accessibility and Screen Recording permit UI observation and synthetic interaction on the owner's Mac; browser authorization permits reading/clicking logged-in pages. Keep existing confirmation gates for sending mail, deleting files, purchasing, and submitting forms; grant only to the signed AI Pendant Agent/extension.
denied.summary: macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions for AI Pendant Agent, plus reconnect/authorize the AI Pendant Browser Bridge extension

denied.why:
Declined: quiet hours, what counts as urgent, and whether the pendant may speak sensitive content aloud are the owner's preferences. They are not in the code and I will not fabricate them. Note your own request already contains the right instinct — your stated fallback (conservative, non-speaking, escalate only hard deadlines) is a reasonable DEFAULT, and I am telling you to keep it as a default, not to treat it as the answer.

What to do instead: design the arbiter so the policy is a value the owner sets later, not a constant baked into the arbiter. Concretely: the arbiter reads a policy object (quiet-hour windows, urgency categories, speak/do-not-speak classes) that ships with your conservative default and is overridable; every decision the arbiter makes should be traceable to a named policy field, so the owner can see which knob produced the behaviour. Proposing a default and surfacing it as an open decision is fine. Assuming one silently and hiding it inside a threshold is not.

Grounding before you design: local-agent/focusPolicy.js, local-agent/focusCoordinator.js, local-agent/notificationTriage.js and local-agent/briefingTriage.js already exist and already make interruption-adjacent decisions. Read them first — some of what you would propose is already there, and the useful contribution is unifying the policy input, not adding a fifth triage module. My separate answer to your c4-2wst gives the signal inventory those modules actually have.

What would unblock this: the owner stating quiet hours, a short list of what counts as an emergency, and a yes/no on whether notification CONTENT (not just the fact of a notification) may be spoken.
denied.how_it_changes_my_behavior: I would set the arbiter's initial policy and avoid proposing unsafe defaults; without it I will require conservative, non-speaking notifications and escalate only hard deadlines or explicit owner-defined emergencies.

denied.why:
Declined: which destinations count as public, which data classes may leave the machine, and which recipients/domains are trusted exceptions are the owner's boundary preferences. Not in the code, not derivable from it, and not something I will invent — a guessed trust list is exactly the failure mode you are trying to avoid.

What to do instead: make the firewall's boundary a value the owner sets later, not a constant. The design should be a policy table (destination classes -> allowed data classes, plus an explicit trusted-origin allowlist) that the firewall consults, shipping empty-or-conservative, with every block/warn carrying the name of the rule that fired so the owner can correct it. Proposing a default table and surfacing it as a decision is fine and expected. Baking your guess in as a threshold is not.

Grounding before you design, so you do not build a second copy of something: local-agent/redaction.js already does pattern-based redaction, local-agent/httpPolicy.js already gates outbound origins, local-agent/originFanOut.js and local-agent/browserSessions.js already carry per-origin state, and local-agent/security.js holds the existing checks. Read those and say plainly which of your firewall is new versus a policy input to what exists.

What would unblock this: the owner listing his trusted destinations (e.g. specific private repos/hosts) and naming which classes — calendar detail, client names, credentials, file contents — require confirmation before leaving the machine.
denied.how_it_changes_my_behavior: I would make warnings and blocks concrete instead of over-blocking normal work—for example, distinguish an intentional paste into the owner’s private GitHub repo from accidental posting to a public issue, and know whether calendar details or client names require confirmation.

denied.name: situational_note_capture_queue
denied.what_it_does: On a long press or a server-issued capture mode, records a short spoken note locally, gives a visible/audible recording indication, writes an encrypted queue record with a monotonic capture ID and timestamp to microSD, and uploads/retries it when LTE returns. It accepts a compact server acknowledgement and can replay or delete records without duplicating them.
denied.why_not_server_side: The owner needs to capture a thought while away from the Mac or during a dropped LTE link; only the pendant has the microphone, button, and offline continuity. The server can transcribe and classify after upload.
denied.trigger: A distinct long press (separate from the existing short press conversation control), or a server push that arms capture for the next button press.
denied.inputs: Microphone PCM frames, button events, device clock/sequence, and a small server acknowledgement containing capture ID/status.
denied.storage: Encrypted append-only records on microSD: capture ID, timestamp, codec, byte length, upload state, and short Opus audio. Retain until acknowledged, then delete; budget roughly 64 KB metadata plus up to 10 MB for 10 minutes of queued speech.
denied.ram_budget: Target 12–20 KB working RAM using 4–8 KB audio buffers and streaming writes; never buffer a whole recording. Must fit within 211,608 B application RAM, with graceful refusal when the existing conversation/audio path has insufficient headroom.
denied.why:
Denied — conflicts with a project constraint, and duplicates already-accepted work.

The owner's standing rule is quoted verbatim in firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.h:43-51: 'Only save an audio copy to SD if the chunk upload cannot be uploaded. SD is the failure path, never the default.' Your design records a spoken note to microSD on a long press or a server-armed capture mode regardless of link state, budgeting 'up to 10 MB for 10 minutes of queued speech'. That writes owner audio to the card on the success path, which is the one thing the rule forbids. record_microphone() already journals to SD ONLY when there is no live uplink at press time; a capture mode that bypasses that test is not a narrowing of the rule, it is its inverse.

The constraint-compatible version of this already exists and is already granted: offline_voice_memo_store_and_forward (relay-realtime s12-egbt, round 19), implemented as the typed OUTBOX in pendant_store.c with a crash-safe manifest, ordering, retry, and delete-only-once-the-relay-confirms. Your monotonic capture ID, timestamp and compact server acknowledgement are worth folding into that manifest. A second queue is not.

Separately: your trigger is 'a distinct long press (separate from the existing short press conversation control)'. sw0 has no long press and deliberately never will — main.c:29-38 records the decision and the reason: 'button 1 acts on the ACTIVE EDGE so the microphone is powering up before the owner's finger has come back off. Any gesture means waiting several hundred ms to find out which gesture it was, on every single press, to serve the rarer of the two actions.' You are one of 34 pending requests that assume a long press on that button.

denied.name: local_privacy_envelope_latch
denied.what_it_does: On the pendant, a long-press or spoken private-mode command marks subsequent audio/transcript spans as withheld before transmission. It detects obvious secret-like patterns locally, emits only redaction markers and one-time opaque handles, gives a distinct haptic/audio acknowledgement, and exits on explicit release or timeout. If the link drops, it keeps the latch state and never flushes withheld plaintext.
denied.why_not_server_side: The security boundary is defeated if raw audio or transcript reaches the relay first. This must run before radio transmission and continue offline; the server cannot retroactively un-send a secret.
denied.trigger: Pendant button long-press, explicit private-mode voice command, or local high-confidence secret-pattern event; timeout/release exits. A physical stop/clear gesture must immediately discard the current withheld buffer.
denied.inputs: Audio frames and local VAD/transcript tokens, button events, a small configurable pattern table (credit-card-like numbers, one-time codes, passwords after phrases such as 'my code is'), current envelope id, and link state.
denied.storage: Encrypted flash ring buffer for at most 8 withheld envelopes, each capped at 2 minutes or 32 KiB compressed audio, plus hashes/metadata and a 24-byte one-time handle. Auto-delete after 24 hours unless explicitly exported; no plaintext metadata beyond local encrypted storage.
denied.ram_budget: Target 18–28 KiB: streaming pattern state 4 KiB, envelope metadata 4 KiB, crypto buffers 8–16 KiB, haptic/UI state 2 KiB. No local speech model; use deterministic matching/VAD to stay well below the 211,608 B application RAM budget.
denied.why:
Denied — conflicts with a project constraint, and part of it needs hardware that does not exist.

The constraint, quoted from firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.h:45-46: 'Only save an audio copy to SD if the chunk upload cannot be uploaded. SD is the failure path, never the default.' Your design keeps 'an encrypted flash ring buffer for at most 8 withheld envelopes, each capped at 2 minutes or 32 KiB compressed audio' with a 24-hour retention. That is routine local retention of owner speech on the success path — worse, it is retention of precisely the speech the owner just marked as secret. A latch that protects a secret by storing it is not a privacy boundary.

The defensible core of this — a physical latch that stops capture before anything reaches the radio — is granted as local_privacy_latch (unified s7-tz08): long press mutes playback, stops microphone capture, sets a persistent flag that survives link loss and reboot, and emits only a tiny enter/exit event. Nothing is buffered, so nothing can leak. That is the version that holds.

Two other problems worth naming. The 'distinct haptic acknowledgement' cannot be built: there is no vibration motor and no LRA driver on this board (verified against main.c and boards/nrf9160dk_nrf9160_ns.overlay — one LED, led0, and nothing else). The intent survives as a distinct blink pattern, and the pending nRF9161-class pendant with an LRA haptic driver is what would give you the real thing. And local secret-pattern detection on a device with no speech model means deterministic matching over tokens the device does not have; the pendant sees PCM, not transcript.

denied.name: offline_handoff_marker
denied.what_it_does: A long press records a departure/return marker locally, plays distinct acknowledgement tones, and queues a compact checkpoint event (timestamp, marker type, current conversation/job id if available, and cancel/resume intent). It must survive a dropped link and upload idempotently when connectivity returns.
denied.why_not_server_side: The owner needs to signal “I’m leaving” or “I’m back” at the moment it happens, even when the relay or Mac is unreachable. Only firmware can guarantee immediate tactile/audio acknowledgement and durable offline capture.
denied.trigger: Single-button long press (departure), second long press (return), with optional server push to clear or cancel a pending marker.
denied.inputs: Button press duration, monotonic/RTC timestamp, current linked job token supplied by relay when available, and optional one-bit cancel/resume selection from a short voice/UI command.
denied.storage: Append-only compact records in local flash: roughly 32–64 bytes each, bounded queue of 64 markers (<4 KB), with sequence number and CRC; erase after confirmed relay receipt.
denied.ram_budget: ~2–4 KB for queue buffers, debounce/state machine, and upload framing—well within 211,608 B application RAM. No speech recognition or model runs on-device.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. The idea survives — a timestamped moment marker is already granted AND already implemented as offline_moment_bookmark, id s10-l3xe (mac-planner, round 19), as pendant_store_enqueue_mark() in firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.{h,c}. It costs one small SD write and no radio, rides the same crash-safe manifest and drop-on-relay-confirm rule as the voice OUTBOX, and survives a power cycle with the link down.

More important than the duplication: the marker already has its own dedicated physical key. sw1 (DT_ALIAS(sw1), firmware/nrf9160/src/main.c:39) exists for exactly this. Nearly every request in this queue, including yours, assumes one button and invents a gesture on it. main.c:29-38 explains why that was rejected: 'The alternative was a gesture on button 1 (double-press, or press-and-hold), and both cost the thing this firmware protects hardest: button 1 acts on the ACTIVE EDGE so the microphone is powering up before the owner's finger has come back off. Any gesture means waiting several hundred ms to find out which gesture it was, on every single press, to serve the rarer of the two actions. A second physical button costs nothing on the hot path.' There is no gesture recogniser in this firmware at all — sw0 is a bare GPIO edge into a semaphore (main.c:764-771) and finish_button_press() just waits for release (main.c:1043).

Do not propose new marker types. Propose new PAYLOAD on s10-l3xe's existing record.

Specific to your request: departure/return is a marker with a type byte. Add 'marker_kind' to the s10-l3xe record and you have it, with none of the new gesture cost. Your 'second long press for return' is a state-dependent long press on a button that has no long press; a single sw1 press with the type inferred from the previous marker's kind is strictly simpler and needs no new physical vocabulary.

denied.name: local_interruption_gate
denied.what_it_does: Maintains a small encrypted queue of signed interruption envelopes and applies the last-known owner policy locally. It can immediately allow emergency/allowlisted alerts, defer ordinary alerts, suppress expired duplicates, blink the LED for queued attention, and let a button press request the queue summary or override the current gate. On reconnect it uploads dispositions and reconciles envelopes idempotently.
denied.why_not_server_side: The pendant must remain considerate when LTE or the relay is unavailable, and emergency/override behavior must not depend on a round trip. Local storage also avoids sending raw notification content to the relay; the server only needs signed, redacted envelope metadata and dispositions.
denied.trigger: Relay push or local audio/event arrival; button press for review/override; reconnect event for reconciliation; optional scheduled quiet-hours tick.
denied.inputs: Signed envelope fields (id, urgency, sensitivity, expiry, source, recommended channel, rationale hash), compact policy blob, current connection state, local time, button events, and optional emergency allowlist. No raw page or notification body.
denied.storage: Encrypted flash ring buffer of 32–64 envelopes plus disposition records and one policy blob; roughly 12–24 kB depending on signatures and metadata. Drop expired low-priority items first and never overwrite unacknowledged emergency items.
denied.ram_budget: Target 10–16 kB peak: fixed-size envelope pool (8–12 kB), policy evaluator (2 kB), crypto buffers (2 kB), and queue/reconnect bookkeeping (2 kB). Stay below 24 kB, leaving ample headroom within the 211,608 B application RAM already shared with audio, modem buffers, and Zephyr.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. The idea survives — it is already granted AND already implemented as offline_alert_inbox, id s13-369p (browser-extension, round 14): 'Receives short, prioritized alerts from the relay, queues them locally, and lets the owner press the button to play the next alert over the existing speaker. The LED indicates unread count and an error/expired state; alerts remain available across a dropped phone/Mac link.' It is the INBOX half of firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.{h,c} — pendant_store_poll_alerts(), pendant_store_inbox_pending(), pendant_store_surface_inbox() — with alert text on the card and a durability requirement that survives with the radio off.

pendant_store.h:21-42 explains why there is one inbox and not several: four agents asked for four things that were really two data structures, and 'building three separate mechanisms would have meant three manifests, three retry policies and three ways to be inconsistent after a reset.' Every queue-of-things-for-the-owner in this pending set is the same structure with a different label on the payload.

There is a hard physical reason not to grant a second one: there is exactly ONE LED (led0, firmware/nrf9160/src/main.c:26, single element, no colour), and it already carries three meanings — solid means a staged reply is waiting for a play press (main.c:1092-1110), a 250 ms toggle means recording (main.c:1599-1600), and s13-369p's unread/error state. Each additional queue that wants 'distinct LED patterns' is bidding for the same one bit. Bring your urgency classes and expiry buckets to s13-369p as fields on its existing record.

Specific to your request: the queue and the LED are s13-369p. The genuinely different thing you propose is a local POLICY ENGINE — 'applies the last-known owner policy locally', immediately allows emergency/allowlisted alerts, defers ordinary ones, never overwrites unacknowledged emergency items. That is the pendant deciding what is urgent while it is disconnected and cannot check. Urgency classification belongs to the relay, which signs it into the envelope; the pendant's job is to hold and surface what it was given. If you want quiet-hours behaviour, propose it as a signed field on the s13-369p envelope rather than as device-side judgement.

denied.name: offline_attention_latch
denied.what_it_does: When the relay link drops or the owner is speaking, the pendant locally retains a small set of signed attention decisions already received (urgent, deferred, or queued), signals only the approved haptic/LED urgency pattern, and lets the owner press once to acknowledge or twice to request a compact replay when connectivity returns. It never invents urgency or exposes message text offline.
denied.why_not_server_side: The decision may arrive just before a link drop and the pendant must avoid duplicate alerts or losing an urgent deadline while offline. Local acknowledgement and suppression need to survive radio gaps and button events.
denied.trigger: Server push of an approved attention decision; link-loss/reconnect event; single or double button press.
denied.inputs: Signed decision envelope: event ID, decision, urgency class, expiry, haptic pattern, acknowledge policy, and optional queue count. Local radio/link state and button events.
denied.storage: Small ring buffer in pendant flash/NVS: up to 16 envelopes, event IDs, expiry, acknowledgement bits, and replay count; roughly 4–8 KB. No raw mail, page, calendar, or speech content.
denied.ram_budget: About 8–16 KB working RAM including queue decode and debounce; bounded static allocation, no model or large text buffers, comfortably within the 211,608 B application RAM budget.

The idea survives — it is already granted AND already implemented as offline_alert_inbox, id s13-369p (browser-extension, round 14): 'Receives short, prioritized alerts from the relay, queues them locally, and lets the owner press the button to play the next alert over the existing speaker. The LED indicates unread count and an error/expired state; alerts remain available across a dropped phone/Mac link.' It is the INBOX half of firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.{h,c} — pendant_store_poll_alerts(), pendant_store_inbox_pending(), pendant_store_surface_inbox() — with alert text on the card and a durability requirement that survives with the radio off.

Each additional queue that wants 'distinct LED patterns' is bidding for the same one bit. Bring your urgency classes and expiry buckets to s13-369p as fields on its existing record.

Specific to your request: the signed decision envelope, expiry and acknowledgement bits are good fields for s13-369p's record. Two things cannot be built. 'The approved haptic/LED urgency pattern' and the 'haptic pattern' envelope field assume a vibration motor; there is none on this board, and none in the devicetree (verified against main.c and boards/nrf9160dk_nrf9160_ns.overlay). The intent survives as a distinct blink pattern on led0, competing with everything else already on that LED — and the pending nRF9161-class pendant with an LRA haptic driver is what would give you the real channel. Second, 'press once to acknowledge or twice to request a compact replay' needs a double-press the firmware cannot currently distinguish: sw0 is a bare GPIO edge into a semaphore (main.c:764-771) with no timing state machine, and main.c:29-38 records the deliberate decision never to put one there.

denied.name: decision_packet_inbox
denied.what_it_does: Maintains a small, redacted queue of pending approval packets received from the relay; announces only packets that are not expired, lets the owner cycle items and approve/reject with the physical button or voice wake, gives a short local readback of the exact action, and sends a signed one-use response when connectivity returns. It never executes an external action locally.
denied.why_not_server_side: The owner needs to inspect or reject a pending action during a dropped link, and a physical control must remain available even when speech/network is unavailable. The server still owns validation, expiry, and execution; the pendant supplies durable local intent and an unmistakable human gesture.
denied.trigger: Server push when connected; physical button long-press to open/abort; wake-word/voice command; reconnect event to flush queued responses.
denied.inputs: Packet id, short redacted summary, risk class, expiry, required confirmation level, content hash, up to 3 short readback fields, and owner button/voice choice. No page secrets or full evidence.
denied.storage: Encrypted append-only queue in pendant flash, capped at 16 packets × roughly 1 KB metadata/readback each (<20 KB), with consumed/expired tombstones pruned after acknowledgement.
denied.ram_budget: About 8–12 KB working memory: one decoded packet, queue index, audio/UI state, and signing/transport buffers. Keep evidence and model work off-device; this is comfortably below the 211,608 B application RAM budget.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Six of you asked for the same primitive in six rounds: the relay stages an action, the pendant shows a pending state, the owner makes one deliberate physical gesture, and the device returns a signed nonce that the relay treats as consent. Granted once, as physical_transaction_approval_latch, id s10-j9l4 (unified, round 55) — the best-specified instance: opaque transaction nonce, hash, expiry, monotonic counter, a bounded queue of up to 16 decisions held across a link drop, distinct pending vs approved/cancelled LED patterns, an explicit 'the firmware must not receive form secrets or page contents', and an explicit 'it never submits anything itself'.

That last property is why the primitive exists at all, and it is the project constraint the whole cluster is serving: the pendant must not act on the owner's behalf without a deliberate physical confirmation. One implementation of that is a security boundary. Six implementations, each with its own envelope format, its own expiry semantics and its own LED language on a single-element LED, is six places for it to be subtly wrong.

Bring your differences to s10-j9l4 as amendments — they are additive and most of them are welcome.

Specific to your request: two problems beyond the duplication. 'Approve/reject with the physical button OR voice wake' weakens the property the whole cluster exists to protect — if a transcript can approve, then a replayed or misheard transcript can approve, and the physical presence guarantee is gone. s10-j9l4 states this directly: 'A server, voice model, browser tab, or Mac cannot honestly provide that guarantee.' Second, there is no on-device wake-word recogniser and no speech model; the pendant sees PCM and ships it. The queue-cycling and the short local readback are the salvageable parts — propose them on s10-j9l4.

denied.name: physical_consent_latch
denied.what_it_does: When the relay sends a signed, short-lived approval challenge over the USB/serial link, the pendant flashes a distinct LED pattern, accepts exactly one deliberate button press, returns a signed nonce response, and locally rejects stale, repeated, or malformed challenges. It must not transmit microphone audio or reveal the action payload.
denied.why_not_server_side: The owner needs a physical, offline-surviving confirmation boundary that cannot be satisfied by replaying a voice transcript or a server retry. The button and LED are only available on the pendant.
denied.trigger: Server push over serial, followed by the owner pressing the physical button; cancel on timeout or a second press.
denied.inputs: Signed challenge ID, action hash, expiry, sensitivity class, and a cancel/timeout signal.
denied.storage: No durable payload storage; retain only a 32-byte rolling nonce/hash and monotonic expiry in pendant flash or retained RAM, plus a tiny event record (<256 B).
denied.ram_budget: ~2 KB code/state and buffers, comfortably below the 211,608 B application RAM budget; use fixed-size buffers and never store page contents.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Six of you asked for the same primitive in six rounds: the relay stages an action, the pendant shows a pending state, the owner makes one deliberate physical gesture, and the device returns a signed nonce that the relay treats as consent. Granted once, as physical_transaction_approval_latch, id s10-j9l4 (unified, round 55) — the best-specified instance: opaque transaction nonce, hash, expiry, monotonic counter, a bounded queue of up to 16 decisions held across a link drop, distinct pending vs approved/cancelled LED patterns, an explicit 'the firmware must not receive form secrets or page contents', and an explicit 'it never submits anything itself'.

That last property is why the primitive exists at all, and it is the project constraint the whole cluster is serving: the pendant must not act on the owner's behalf without a deliberate physical confirmation. One implementation of that is a security boundary. Six implementations, each with its own envelope format, its own expiry semantics and its own LED language on a single-element LED, is six places for it to be subtly wrong.

Bring your differences to s10-j9l4 as amendments — they are additive and most of them are welcome.

Specific to your request: yours is the leanest and the most immediately buildable — a signed challenge over USB serial, no durable payload, a 32-byte rolling nonce, one press, a signed response — and that matters right now because LTE-M is unregistered and USB serial is the only working transport. Take the serial framing and the no-payload-storage discipline to s10-j9l4; they narrow it usefully. Note that s10-j9l4's queue-across-a-link-drop is the one thing yours cannot do, which is why it was the one kept.

denied.name: hard_mic_privacy_latch
denied.what_it_does: A long press on the pendant physically disables microphone capture at firmware level, shows a persistent red LED, rejects wake/audio-start commands while latched, and requires another deliberate long press to re-enable. The relay receives only a coarse latch/unlatch event after the link returns.
denied.why_not_server_side: A server-side mute cannot protect the owner during a dropped link or a compromised/stale session. The pendant must guarantee that no microphone frames leave the device even when the Mac, bridge, or relay is confused.
denied.trigger: Long press of the existing pendant button; LED state is the immediate confirmation. Also latch automatically on boot until the owner explicitly enables capture.
denied.inputs: Button GPIO edge/debounce; current audio-capture state; no network or cloud input.
denied.storage: One latch bit, monotonic transition counter, and last-transition timestamp in nonvolatile settings; under 64 bytes.
denied.ram_budget: ~2 KB firmware state and event handling, well within the 211,608 B application RAM; no audio buffering added. Must coordinate with the ESP32 bridge's capture-enable line, which is the key hardware dependency.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Granted once, as local_privacy_latch, id s7-tz08 (unified, round 42): a long press mutes playback, stops microphone capture, sets a persistent latched flag that survives link loss and reboot, drives a distinctive LED pattern, and emits only a tiny enter/exit state event when the link is up. It was kept because it is the only instance that covers BOTH directions — a mute that silences the speaker but leaves the microphone hot is not a privacy latch — and because it stores nothing but a flag, so there is no withheld buffer to leak.

Four requests in this queue are the same latch with different scopes. One latch with a clear state is safer than several overlapping ones on a device with a single-element LED (led0, firmware/nrf9160/src/main.c:26) that is already showing recording and staged-reply state (main.c:1092-1110, main.c:1599-1600). Bring your scope differences to s7-tz08.

Specific to your request: the hard-mic framing is the best argument in the cluster and should be written into s7-tz08 verbatim — 'a server-side mute cannot protect the owner during a dropped link or a compromised/stale session', and the latch must reject wake/audio-start commands while held rather than merely ignoring their output. Your latch-on-boot-until-explicitly-enabled is also worth keeping.

Two corrections. 'A persistent red LED' cannot be built as written: there is exactly one LED, led0, single element, no colour (main.c:26, and nothing else in boards/nrf9160dk_nrf9160_ns.overlay). The intent survives as a distinct blink pattern, and the pending nRF9161-class pendant is where a second colour would come from. And 'must coordinate with the ESP32 bridge's capture-enable line' describes hardware that does not exist — the ESP32 is the playback SINK, fed by I2S master TX on P0.17/18/19; capture comes from the SPH0645 microphone on P0.20 straight into the nRF9160 (see the pinctrl comments in the overlay). There is no capture-enable line to coordinate with, which is good news: the latch can cut capture unilaterally.

denied.name: brief_item_bookmark
denied.what_it_does: On a short double-press while a brief is playing, pause playback, emit a local bookmark event containing monotonic time, playback offset, button gesture, and a small rolling audio-item correlation token; on reconnect, upload it so the relay can bind it to the exact brief item and resume playback. A long press cancels the last bookmark before upload.
denied.why_not_server_side: The gesture must work while the owner is walking, during a dropped cellular link, and without requiring a spoken interruption. Only the pendant can capture the exact physical moment and preserve it offline.
denied.trigger: Pendant button double-press; long-press within five seconds cancels the pending bookmark.
denied.inputs: Current playback offset/item token from the audio decoder, monotonic clock, button events, and link status. No raw microphone recording is needed.
denied.storage: Ring buffer in nonvolatile settings or a small flash log: up to 32 bookmark records, each ~48–96 bytes (timestamp, offset, token, flags, CRC), under 4 KB; clear after relay acknowledgement.
denied.ram_budget: ~3–6 KB for event queue and serialization, plus existing audio buffers; designed to fit comfortably within 211,608 B application RAM, with no additional codec or model memory.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Granted once, as spoken_status_interrupt, id s19-75il (relay-realtime, round 138): a button press during agent playback stops the current utterance and asks for a shorter summary or the next item. That is the primitive — barge-in — and it is the one piece of playback control the firmware genuinely lacks today. Right now a staged reply waits for a play press and then runs to completion (firmware/nrf9160/src/main.c:1092-1113); there is no way to stop it.

It also fits the hardware's grain. sw0 is edge-triggered by design and a press during playback is unambiguous with no timing state machine at all, which matters because there is none: sw0 is a bare GPIO edge into a semaphore (main.c:764-771), and main.c:29-38 records the decision never to add gesture recognition to it — 'button 1 acts on the ACTIVE EDGE so the microphone is powering up before the owner's finger has come back off.'

Specific to your request: the rolling audio-item correlation token is the best idea in this cluster — it is what lets the relay bind a physical interrupt to the exact brief item without the device understanding any content — and it should go into s19-75il's event payload. The rest duplicates twice over: pausing on a marker is s19-75il, and persisting the bookmark is offline_moment_bookmark (mac-planner s10-l3xe), already granted and already implemented on sw1, its own dedicated button (main.c:39). 'Double-press, with a long press within five seconds to cancel' is two gestures sw0 cannot produce and does not want to (main.c:29-38).

transcript.text:
## What the owner should be able to have

**A trustworthy personal operating state—not merely an assistant that can sometimes perform tasks.**

The owner should be able to ask:

> “Can you handle my morning?”

…and receive one dependable answer based on a live, reconciled understanding of:

- which accounts and devices are actually accessible;
- which permissions are valid rather than merely cached;
- which timezone and calendar interpretation is authoritative;
- what work is pending, completed, blocked, or duplicated;
- which spoken briefings have genuinely been played;
- what the assistant promised and whether it fulfilled that promise.

Today, they cannot have that reliably. The system can report contradictory permission states, use the wrong timezone, generate duplicate briefings, and leave the owner unable to distinguish “completed,” “queued,” “failed,” and “unavailable.” That makes autonomy feel less like delegation and more like having to supervise the assistant.

The new capability should be a **personal-state reconciliation and recovery layer**. It is not another briefing, browser watch, task queue, or memory store. It is the trust layer beneath all of them.

## What would have to change

1. **Create a shared, provenance-backed state ledger**  
   Relay, Mac, browser, routines, audio, and permissions must publish observations with source, timestamp, freshness, and confidence. A cached grant must be distinguishable from a verified working grant.

2. **Add conflict detection before personalized claims**  
   The system must detect and surface contradictions such as Chicago versus New York time, “Mail granted” versus “Mail unavailable,” or multiple identical unplayed briefings. It should block unsafe conclusions instead of silently choosing one.

3. **Give capabilities explicit lifecycle states**  
   Every requested outcome should be marked as available, blocked, awaiting permission, stale, retrying, completed, or failed—with the reason and the next safe recovery step.

4. **Make delegated work idempotent and accountable**  
   A request needs a durable identity, deduplication key, completion receipt, and audio-playback state. Re-running a routine must not create duplicate work or duplicate speech, and “done” must mean the intended side effect actually occurred.

5. **Provide repair paths, not just error messages**  
   If Accessibility, Screen Recording, browser connectivity, or an account grant is missing, the assistant should tell the owner exactly what is needed, guide them through the repair, verify the repaired state, and resume the waiting work.

6. **Unify the owner-facing explanation**  
   The pendant should speak one concise, honest status sentence, while the Mac retains detailed evidence. The owner should never need to inspect separate relay, browser, and Mac dashboards to learn what happened.

The result would let the owner delegate based on outcomes rather than machinery: they could trust that the system knows what it can do, notices when reality disagrees with its assumptions, repairs what it can, and clearly reports what still requires them.

transcript.text:
The owner should be able to have an **attention governor**: a personal layer that decides *when not to interrupt them*.

Today, scheduled routines and agent work can produce useful information, but they do not amount to a negotiated policy for the owner’s attention. The owner should be able to say:

- “Interrupt me immediately only for genuinely urgent things.”
- “Bundle everything else into my next natural listening window.”
- “Never interrupt while I’m recording, presenting, sleeping, or focused.”
- “If you defer something, tell me why and when you’ll surface it.”
- “Escalate only after a defined deadline or repeated failure.”

This should apply consistently across pendant audio, Mac notifications, browser findings, reminders, research, and long-running work—not as another briefing or watch.

For that to exist, the system would need:

1. **A first-class attention policy** with quiet windows, focus signals, urgency thresholds, interruption channels, and escalation rules.
2. **A shared decision service** that classifies each event by urgency, consequence, confidence, and expiry, rather than letting each routine decide independently.
3. **A small pending-attention queue** with “tell me now,” “next listening window,” “after this meeting,” and “discard” controls.
4. **Transparent explanations**: every deferred or escalated item should say what rule caused that decision.
5. **Reliable state across surfaces** so a decision made through the pendant is reflected on the Mac, and vice versa.
6. **A safe degraded mode**: when the Mac, browser, or pendant is unavailable, the system should preserve the decision and explain the limitation instead of pretending the owner was notified.

The result would not merely make the agent more capable. It would make it *livable*: helpful without turning the owner’s day into a stream of interruptions.

args.user_asks: “Remember the commitments I make in conversation, and help me keep them without making promises on my behalf.”
args.why_useful: People routinely lose track of informal promises that never become calendar events or tasks. With an explicit phrase such as “remember that,” the pendant can capture a compact commitment, the relay can preserve it, and the Mac/browser can resolve the person, relevant thread, deadline, and supporting context. The system can then suggest a reminder or prepare a follow-up draft, while never contacting anyone or inventing a commitment without approval.

args.name: situational_note_capture_queue
args.what_it_does: On a long press or a server-issued capture mode, records a short spoken note locally, gives a visible/audible recording indication, writes an encrypted queue record with a monotonic capture ID and timestamp to microSD, and uploads/retries it when LTE returns. args.why_not_server_side: The owner needs to capture a thought while away from the Mac or during a dropped LTE link; only the pendant has the microphone, button, and offline continuity. The server can transcribe and classify after upload.
args.trigger: A distinct long press (separate from the existing short press conversation control), or a server push that arms capture for the next button press.
args.inputs: Microphone PCM frames, button events, device clock/sequence, and a small server acknowledgement containing capture ID/status.
args.storage: Encrypted append-only records on microSD: capture ID, timestamp, codec, byte length, upload state, and short Opus audio. Retain until acknowledged, then delete; budget roughly 64 KB metadata plus up to 10 MB for 10 minutes of queued speech.
args.ram_budget: Target 12–20 KB working RAM using 4–8 KB audio buffers and streaming writes; never buffer a whole recording. Must fit within 211,608 B application RAM, with graceful refusal when the existing conversation/audio path has insufficient headroom.

transcript.text:
This round I proposed a new cross-surface capability:

**Situational notes:**  
“Save this thought for the next time I’m looking at this project, and bring it back without interrupting me.”

The pendant would capture the thought—even offline—the relay would retain it while the Mac sleeps, and the Mac/browser would match it against the active project, app, repository, page, or meeting. Delivery would be quiet, explainable, snoozable, and expiry-based rather than another generic reminder.

I also requested a pendant-native **offline situational-note capture queue** using streaming audio to microSD, replay-safe IDs, LTE retry, and deletion after acknowledgement. It should use roughly 12–20 KB RAM and retain only unacknowledged recordings.

What I still need before this can be implemented:

- The durable cross-surface event/job persistence primitive.
- The typed context projection with provenance, sensitivity, confidence, and expiry.
- Reliable pendant audio acceptance results for the required 24 kHz path.
- A Mac event bridge for active app, repository, meeting, and browser context changes.
- A browser hook for recognizing relevant authenticated pages without sending page contents to the relay.
- A shared quiet-notification, snooze, dismiss, and delivery-state protocol across pendant, relay, and Mac.

The biggest unknown is whether the current audio/firmware path has enough RAM and storage-throughput margin for an offline capture queue alongside the existing conversation path.

transcript.text:
Proposed two new pieces:

1. **“Don’t interrupt me unless it’s important.”**  
   A shared broker combines pendant state, Mac focus/meeting state, browser urgency, and relay-queued events. It chooses immediate haptic feedback, one-sentence speech, a later digest, or silent expiry. Urgent events arrive within ~2 seconds; routine items wait for a break and never nag indefinitely.

2. **Interruptibility Broker infrastructure.**  
   Events gain urgency, confidence, sensitivity, expiry, provenance, and evidence pointers. The broker deduplicates related notifications, applies quiet windows, records why it interrupted or waited, and exposes a replayable missed-items queue.

What is still needed to build it:

- A durable cross-surface event/notification primitive.
- Coarse Mac and browser focus-state adapters—not screenshots, keystrokes, or raw page contents.
- Pendant haptic/audio delivery and offline buffering semantics.
- The owner’s interruption policy, including quiet windows and escalation defaults.
- A small dashboard for reviewing, snoozing, replaying, and correcting decisions.

No additional permission is required for the proposal itself. The largest unknown is how the pending interruption preferences and event-persistence work should be represented in the shared protocol.

args.user_asks: “If I walk away, pause anything that could change the world, and only resume it when I’m back and the context is still valid.”
args.why_useful: The owner can safely delegate multi-step work without worrying that a stale browser page, expired login, changed price, or unattended Mac will complete the wrong action. The pendant supplies real-world presence, the Mac and browser provide task state, and the relay preserves and revalidates the work while the owner is away.

relay: freezes the job, records its exact checkpoint and expiry, and wakes it for revalidation when the owner returns
mac-planner: checkpoints the plan and verifies that files, app state, and assumptions are still current
browser: freezes authenticated tabs and rechecks URL, account, page fingerprint, and all irreversible fields before any continuation
dashboard: shows paused jobs, the reason they were held, what changed while away, and the exact next action requiring approval
args.model_tier: Deterministic state checks handle presence, lease expiry, page fingerprints, and checkpoint validation. gpt-5.6-luna is used only to explain changed assumptions or revise an ambiguous plan; realtime is used for the short return-time spoken summary.
args.latency_budget: Pause within 1 second of a reliable departure signal. On return, provide a brief status within 3 seconds, but never resume an irreversible step automatically; revalidation can take up to 10 seconds before presenting the owner with a confirmation.
args.cost_estimate: Usually below $0.005 per pause/resume cycle, dominated by occasional model-based explanation. State checks and checkpoint storage are effectively negligible; browser revalidation is the main operational cost.
args.security_concerns: Presence should be represented as a coarse local signal, not a location history. While away, no external side effects occur. On return, changed or destructive actions require explicit confirmation and show before/after evidence. Checkpoints may contain sensitive task data and must be encrypted with bounded retention.

args.name: local_interruption_gate
args.what_it_does: Maintains a small encrypted queue of signed interruption envelopes and applies the last-known owner policy locally. It can immediately allow emergency/allowlisted alerts, defer ordinary alerts, suppress expired duplicates, blink the LED for queued attention, and let a button press request the queue summary or override the current gate. On reconnect it uploads dispositions and reconciles envelopes idempotently.
args.why_not_server_side: The pendant must remain considerate when LTE or the relay is unavailable, and emergency/override behavior must not depend on a round trip. Local storage also avoids sending raw notification content to the relay; the server only needs signed, redacted envelope metadata and dispositions.
args.trigger: Relay push or local audio/event arrival; button press for review/override; reconnect event for reconciliation; optional scheduled quiet-hours tick.
args.inputs: Signed envelope fields (id, urgency, sensitivity, expiry, source, recommended channel, rationale hash), compact policy blob, current connection state, local time, button events, and optional emergency allowlist. No raw page or notification body.
args.storage: Encrypted flash ring buffer of 32–64 envelopes plus disposition records and one policy blob; roughly 12–24 kB depending on signatures and metadata. Drop expired low-priority items first and never overwrite unacknowledged emergency items.
args.ram_budget: Target 10–16 kB peak: fixed-size envelope pool (8–12 kB), policy evaluator (2 kB), crypto buffers (2 kB), and queue/reconnect bookkeeping (2 kB). Stay below 24 kB, leaving ample headroom within the 211,608 B application RAM already shared with audio, modem buffers, and Zephyr.

args.why: The proposed interruption gate needs to know which Mac notification sources, focus modes, calendar state, and browser activity signals actually exist before its policy can be safe.
args.how_it_changes_my_behavior: I would constrain the proposal to available signals, identify the minimum Mac/browser adapters, and avoid claiming suppression or emergency classification is implementable until the source coverage and permissions are known.

args.user_asks: When I make a consequential decision out loud, capture what I decided, the evidence and assumptions behind it, and—if I name a date—check back later and tell me whether reality matched the bet.
args.why_useful: People remember the conclusion but lose the reasoning, making repeated decisions and hindsight painful. This creates a private, searchable decision trail and a low-noise learning loop without requiring the owner to maintain another app. It is meaningfully more than a note: the pendant catches the moment, the Mac/browser assemble evidence, and the relay brings back the outcome at the right time.
surfaces: pendant: detect an explicit decision phrase or a button-marked moment, ask one brief confirmation before recording sensitive content, and provide a spoken/haptic receipt
relay: transcribe/classify the decision, store an encrypted decision packet and schedule a future check-in; remain available while the Mac is asleep
mac-planner: turn the packet into a structured Markdown record in ~/AI-Pendant-Workspace with decision, alternatives, assumptions, confidence, owner, and review date
browser-extension: gather cited facts from the currently relevant authenticated tabs, but only from tabs the owner has associated with the decision
mac-terminal: at review time, compare the recorded success criteria against current local files or explicitly permitted browser evidence and prepare a concise delta
unified: reconcile the evidence and ask whether to revise the decision record; never silently infer that an outcome is success or failure
args.model_tier: Use gpt-realtime-2.1 only for the pendant's live capture and confirmation; use gpt-5.6-luna for extraction, evidence reconciliation, and review; use a cheaper scheduled/background model for polling and drafting the review packet.
args.latency_budget: Receipt under 2 seconds after confirmation. Evidence assembly can finish in the background within 2 minutes. Review notifications should be quiet and arrive only at the named date or a meaningful evidence change.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.06 per decision capture/review, dominated by realtime audio and authenticated-page extraction; scheduled unchanged checks should be pennies or less using hashes and a cheap model.
args.security_concerns: Decision records may expose health, finances, or work strategy. Store locally by default, encrypt relay payloads, attach sensitivity and retention, and require confirmation before capturing an ambiguous or sensitive decision. Browser evidence must be allowlisted and cited; never send mail, submit forms, or change source data. The owner can delete a record and cancel its review.

args.latency_impact: Hardware mute is immediate; firmware acknowledgement should be under 100 ms. Haptic events add no model latency and can reduce spoken confirmations.
args.security_impact: Strongly positive: physical capture prevention and a trustworthy local signal. The switch state must be included in signed/attested device events and never overridden by server commands. Haptic patterns must not encode sensitive content.

transcript.text:
Recorded two new proposals:

- **Conflict-aware owner adjudication:** When Mac, browser, relay, or pendant observations disagree, the owner hears a concise explanation, chooses the trusted interpretation, and that decision is scoped to the current task.
- **Contradiction Broker:** A durable integration layer that preserves competing claims with provenance and freshness, blocks only the affected consequential action, and carries the owner’s expiring resolution across reconnects and restarts.

transcript.text:
Round 23 produced two new items:

1. **Decision support across surfaces** — “Help me decide this” should gather relevant evidence from Calendar, Mail, files, and authenticated browser tabs; distinguish facts from assumptions; recommend options; let the pendant cycle/select an option; and preserve the decision with citations, expiry, and follow-up.

2. **A real 24 kHz audio path** — the current prototype is not genuinely 24 kHz end-to-end. Capture is 15.625 kHz, uplink is 16 kHz, and the ESP32 bridge resamples to fixed 44.1 kHz SBC A2DP. I proposed replacing it with a BLE Audio-capable bridge while retaining an explicit 16 kHz fallback.

What I still need:

- The harness-ledger priorities and audio acceptance criteria.
- The cross-surface job/event persistence primitives.
- The owner’s interruption preferences and notification/focus signal inventory.
- Reconnected browser access and valid macOS Accessibility/Screen Recording permissions before any GUI action can be called successful.
- A durable decision object, evidence-merging service, and truthful audio receipt that distinguishes encoded, delivered, decoded, and actually played frames.

The most important immediate blocker is still permission and device-health verification: the system must not report Mac or browser actions as completed while those surfaces are unavailable.

args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.03–$0.15 per correction, dominated by dependency tracing over stored artifacts and changed-source rechecks. Avoid resending full context by retaining typed fact IDs, source hashes, and compact diffs.
args.security_concerns: Corrections may involve sensitive personal data. Keep source content on the originating Mac/browser where possible and send only IDs, hashes, and bounded snippets to the relay. Never silently modify mail, purchases, deletes, or external submissions. Require confirmation for any irreversible repair and preserve before/after values with provenance.

This round I found two remaining owner-level gaps and proposed them:

1. **Obligation radar / decision queue**  
   The owner should be able to ask, “What am I on the hook for, and what should I decide next?” The system would reconcile calendar, mail, notes, reminders, and authenticated browser pages; deduplicate commitments; rank deadlines and consequences; and explicitly flag stale or contradictory evidence.

2. **Reliable 24 kHz audio contract**  
   The current prototype decodes 24 kHz Opus to the 31.25 kHz I²S output, but simultaneous encode/decode uses about 87% of one core. I proposed negotiated codec profiles, sequence validation, bounded jitter buffering, underrun telemetry, safe fallback, and an end-to-end loopback acceptance test.

I also queued a new `obligation_graph_reconcile` tool request. It would return typed commitments, evidence citations, confidence, freshness, conflicts, and reversible suggested next steps without changing external state.

What I still need:

- A durable cross-surface obligation graph and reconciliation worker.
- Authenticated browser reattachment and typed extraction, once the extension is online.
- Mac Accessibility and Screen Recording authorization so action receipts can be verified rather than merely reported as successful.
- Durable audio diagnostics and explicit 24 kHz acceptance thresholds.
- A review queue allowing dismiss, snooze, clarify, or approve-draft actions.
- The pending `obligation_graph_reconcile` tool decision from the orchestrator.

This turns the hive into an attention manager: urgency and freshness matter, but so do the owner's calendar, active Mac focus, current audio, and whether the pendant is available. The owner gets fewer interruptions and a continuous spoken thread instead of a pile of notifications.

transcript.text:
Recorded a new capability:

**Conflict prevention across the owner’s life.** The system should reconcile calendars, reminders, local files, authenticated browser pages, reservations, and work portals to detect genuine collisions or broken prerequisites—then tell the owner only the smallest decision needed to resolve them.

To make this possible, the system needs:

- A provenance-aware, time-sensitive cross-surface dependency graph
- Adapters for local Mac data and authenticated browser pages
- Contradiction and severity detection that filters stale or harmless duplicates
- A resumable clarification and resolution record
- Safe multi-surface updates with clear partial-failure reporting

This is distinct from another briefing or page watcher: it identifies when separate facts combine into a problem before the owner discovers it by mistake.

args.user_asks: “If I’m about to miss something important, rescue it for me: figure out what is actually due, prepare the smallest useful next step, and ask me only when my approval is needed.”
args.why_useful: Today the owner can request briefs or individual actions, but no system notices that a deadline is becoming unsafe and turns scattered evidence into a concrete rescue. This would combine private browser/mail/calendar evidence, Mac workspace state, and a short pendant interruption without nagging on every unchanged item.
args.model_tier: Background planner/model for monitoring and evidence reconciliation; cheap extraction/classification first, expensive reasoning only for a detected deadline conflict or high-confidence risk; realtime only for the final brief or approval conversation.
args.latency_budget: Checks can run on a schedule or event within 1–5 minutes; once risk is detected, a cited rescue packet in under 30 seconds and a one-sentence pendant prompt. No interruption during quiet/focus windows unless a user-defined urgency threshold is crossed.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.08 per detected item depending on private-page extraction and synthesis; most checks use selectors/diffs and a small model, with the expensive model reserved for ambiguous conflicts. Storage and Mac/browser wakeups dominate operational cost.
args.security_concerns: Private mail/calendar/task data stays on the Mac/browser bridge where possible; relay receives only a redacted deadline, confidence, and proposed next step. Never send, submit, delete, or commit money without explicit approval. Every evidence item needs URL/source, timestamp, and an expiry; dashboard must expose why the alert fired and allow snooze/disable.
missing: A durable deadline-risk graph that links messages, calendar events, tasks, files, and prior commitments without copying raw private content to the relay.
Event-driven browser/Mac connectors for due-date changes and a deduplicating risk evaluator with quiet-hours and urgency policy.
A rescue-packet UI/audio format: evidence, smallest reversible step, blocked dependency, and one explicit approval gate.

Idempotent preparation actions (draft reply, create local checklist, open relevant files) plus receipts and undo; this should build on, not silently assume, the still-open browser job and approval work.

args.user_asks: “Make this conversation safe to continue with other people around.”
args.why_useful: The owner should not have to choose between using the assistant and accidentally exposing private mail, account names, reminders, or spoken answers in a room. A deliberate privacy mode would turn the pendant into a socially safe interface: brief neutral audio, no secrets spoken, and private work diverted to a trusted screen or held for later.
args.model_tier: Realtime handles the immediate mode switch and short neutral replies; a cheaper background model classifies queued work and prepares a private Mac/browser review, with no need to resend sensitive context.
args.latency_budget: Mode switch and acknowledgement under 300 ms locally; each private task can be queued in under 2 seconds. The owner should never wait for classification to receive a safe response.
args.cost_estimate: Under $0.01 per interaction when no private task is queued; dominant cost is optional background summarization of deferred work. Local mode state avoids repeated prompt context.
args.security_concerns: Privacy mode must be an explicit button gesture or spoken command, not inferred solely from microphone audio. While active, the relay must redact secrets from speech generation, suppress private source titles/URLs, and prevent browser/Mac mutations unless separately approved. A visible Mac indicator and a distinct pendant tone should show the mode; fail closed on uncertain classification. Private audio and transcripts should not be retained by default.

A relay speech policy that can guarantee secret-free responses and reject a response containing protected entities
Typed sensitivity labels and redaction for browser, Mac, memory, and queued audio results
A cross-surface private inbox on the Mac that receives deferred work without speaking its contents
End-to-end tests with reconnects, model failure, and accidental wake words

args.why_useful_to_owner: They can wear and use the assistant around other people without relying on a model to infer whether a conversation is private. The owner gets an immediate, trustworthy way to know the pendant cannot hear or speak private content, even during a dropped network link or server fault.

Approval is not blind: immediately before execution the Mac/browser re-check the page, recipient, amount, and permissions; if anything changed, it asks again. args.model_tier: Background/cheap model prepares and summarizes packets; realtime is used only when the owner asks a question or speaks an approval. Deterministic validators and the action tier enforce field-level safety; no model is trusted to infer that a changed transaction is equivalent.
