args.user_asks: “Show me what I knew, what I had promised, and what changed when I made that decision.”
args.why_useful: Today the owner can get current facts or an action receipt, but not reconstruct the state of their life at the moment a decision was made. A provenance-preserving time slice would let them revisit a missed commitment, disputed detail, or forgotten rationale without relying on memory: the pendant’s spoken context, relay events, Mac files/calendar, and authenticated browser evidence are aligned into a dated, uncertainty-labeled snapshot.
args.model_tier: Use a cheap background model to index and summarize already-captured records; use the realtime tier only when the owner asks a spoken follow-up. Retrieval should return citations and quoted evidence before any interpretation.
args.latency_budget: Return a first compact timeline in 2–5 seconds from indexed records, then progressively add Mac/browser evidence within 30 seconds. No live crawling is needed unless the owner explicitly asks for a current comparison.
args.cost_estimate: Low ongoing indexing cost and roughly $0.005–$0.03 per reconstruction depending on the number of records; storage/indexing and provenance joins dominate, not realtime inference.
args.security_concerns: This is unusually sensitive: snapshots may expose private audio, mail, calendar, browser pages, and secrets. Store structured facts and short evidence spans with strict TTLs, source sensitivity labels, per-surface inclusion controls, and deletion propagation. Never present inferred motives as facts; distinguish captured evidence, absent evidence, and model synthesis. Require confirmation before sharing or exporting a snapshot.
missing: An append-only, timestamped cross-surface evidence ledger that preserves event IDs, source, freshness, and deletion links
A queryable time-slice compiler that can answer “as of” questions without silently substituting current values
Retention and redaction controls spanning R2 audio, D1 jobs/memory, Mac workspace artifacts, and browser inspection records
A review view/audio format that speaks uncertainty and cites the original source without replaying sensitive audio by default

args.user_asks: “Before I act on an important detail, tell me if my sources disagree—and show me the smallest thing I can check to resolve it.”
args.why_useful: Current assistants summarize sources, but can quietly blend a stale calendar entry, an email, and a logged-in webpage into a confident false answer. The owner should receive a contradiction alert: exactly which claims conflict, which source is newer or more authoritative, what remains unknown, and one reversible verification step. This is especially valuable for appointments, travel, payments, deadlines, and addresses.
args.model_tier: Cheap background extraction normalizes claims and compares them; realtime is reserved for speaking the concise conflict and asking whether to verify. No model should resolve a conflict by plausibility alone.
args.latency_budget: For an explicit question, speak a provisional conflict notice within 2 seconds and complete read-only verification in under 30 seconds. Passive checks run asynchronously and notify only high-impact contradictions.
args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.002–$0.02 per comparison; extraction and source reads dominate. Deduplicate unchanged claims and use hashes so routine checks are nearly free.
args.security_concerns: Claim records may contain sensitive account, travel, or health information. Keep source snippets bounded, label sensitivity, redact secrets, and avoid reading a private source unless the owner’s request authorizes it. Verification must be read-only by default; any correction or submission requires the existing confirmation policy.
missing: A typed claim/contradiction graph with source authority, timestamps, confidence, and materiality
A cross-surface read planner that can re-check only the conflicting fields in Mac, browser, and relay records
An impact policy that distinguishes harmless wording differences from conflicts capable of causing missed deadlines or financial harm
A concise pendant conflict-card/audio format with a one-step verification action and explicit uncertainty

args.user_asks: When a meeting starts, quietly get me ready, help me capture commitments during it, and leave me a reviewable follow-up packet afterward.
args.why_useful: Today preparation, live capture, and follow-up are disconnected. This would turn the pendant into a low-friction meeting companion: it uses the Mac's calendar and private browser context for preparation, the pendant for discreet capture while walking or away from the keyboard, and the relay to finish the packet after the meeting. It never sends anything without approval.
surfaces: mac-planner reads the next calendar event and gathers its agenda, attendees, related notes, and open browser tabs; browser-extension reads only already-open authenticated tabs relevant to that event and cites each fact; relay-realtime gives a brief spoken or LED-only pre-meeting cue and accepts short pendant utterances such as “commitment: send the estimate Friday” or “park that”; unified correlates utterances with the meeting's time window and participant context; mac-planner writes a dated meeting packet into ~/AI-Pendant-Workspace containing decisions, commitments, owners, due dates, unresolved questions, evidence links, and confidence; pendant plays a short post-meeting summary when the owner is available.
args.model_tier: Use the cheaper background model for pre-meeting retrieval, transcript cleanup, deduplication, and packet assembly; reserve realtime only for the brief cue and live utterance acknowledgement. Escalate to the expensive judgement tier only when owner, due date, or commitment attribution is ambiguous.
args.latency_budget: Pre-meeting packet ready 2 minutes before the event or on explicit request; pendant acknowledgement under 1 second; post-meeting packet within 2 minutes of the event ending. If calendar/browser access is unavailable, produce a clearly incomplete packet rather than inventing facts.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.01–$0.05 per meeting for background extraction and summarization, depending on transcript length; realtime cost is limited to a few short turns. Mac and browser work dominate operational complexity, not tokens.
args.security_concerns: Meeting speech and private-tab data may leave the device to the relay/model, so default to local Mac notes and redact unrelated tab content. Do not infer or expose attendee-sensitive details beyond the meeting packet. Require explicit approval before sending follow-up email, creating external tickets, or changing calendar events; show source snippets and proposed recipients.
missing: A calendar-event identity and time-window correlation service shared by relay, Mac, and browser
A pendant capture mode that queues timestamped utterances offline and syncs them when the link returns
A meeting packet schema with provenance, confidence, owner/due-date fields, and a review UI
A reliable post-event trigger and availability check so the summary is not spoken during another conversation

args.change: Add a durable Meeting Episode Coordinator spanning calendar event IDs, browser tab/session provenance, pendant utterance timestamps, and Mac packet files. It opens an episode shortly before an event, accepts append-only capture records during the event (including offline records with monotonic sequence numbers), closes it at event end, and emits a reviewable packet with every claim linked to its source or explicitly marked owner-spoken. Reopening an episode is idempotent; unrelated tabs and speech are excluded by default.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can say a commitment once while their hands are busy and later find exactly what was decided, who owns it, and why the system believes it—without trusting a vague AI summary or losing notes when the network drops.
args.effort: Medium-high: shared event identity and lifecycle service, pendant queue/sync protocol, Mac packet renderer, and tests for overlapping meetings, timezone changes, missed close events, and duplicate delivery.
args.risk: A wrong calendar match could attach private notes to the wrong meeting. Fail closed when identity or timing is ambiguous, show the event title before capture begins, encrypt local records, and retain append-only raw captures only briefly. If closure fails, leave the episode explicitly open rather than silently summarizing.
args.cost_impact: Small persistent metadata and local file storage; background model calls roughly $0.01–$0.05 per meeting. Pendant firmware adds a bounded queue, likely tens of KB, with no meaningful ongoing power cost beyond normal radio sync.
args.latency_impact: Capture acknowledgement remains sub-second; packet assembly can complete asynchronously within two minutes. Offline utterances become visible after reconnect rather than being dropped.
args.security_impact: Calendar titles, attendee names, and spoken commitments are sensitive. Use event-scoped least-privilege projections, redact unrelated browser content, encrypt queued captures, and require approval for any outbound follow-up.
depends_on: A shared durable event/episode identifier across relay and Mac
An offline pendant capture queue and reconnect protocol
A provenance-aware meeting packet schema and review surface
A post-event trigger plus owner availability/quiet-hours check

args.user_asks: Before I commit to a time, deadline, or promise anywhere, quietly tell me if it will make another commitment impossible and suggest the safest wording or alternative.
args.why_useful: People often make commitments in separate contexts—an email, a calendar invite, a private portal, or a conversation—and only discover the collision afterward. This would give the owner a last-second, evidence-backed judgment before a promise becomes real, while leaving the final decision with them.
surfaces: browser-extension detects a proposed date, deadline, recipient, or submission in the currently active authenticated page without submitting it; mac-planner checks Calendar, reminders, travel context, and existing reviewable commitments; relay holds a short-lived cross-surface conflict assessment and sends a discreet spoken or LED warning through the pendant when confidence is high; unified presents two or three feasible alternatives with the exact conflicting sources; browser or Mac fills only the chosen revised wording/time after explicit owner approval, then stores a receipt.
args.model_tier: Use a cheap background model to normalize dates and compare candidate times. Use the realtime tier only when the owner is actively composing or speaking and needs an immediate warning. Escalate ambiguous interpretation to judgement rather than silently blocking.
args.latency_budget: Warn within 1–2 seconds of a detected candidate commitment; if evidence is incomplete, say so and do not interrupt. A detailed alternative list may arrive asynchronously before submission.
args.cost_estimate: Under $0.01 for most checks with compact structured context; occasional long-page extraction may cost $0.03–$0.08. The dominant cost is private-context retrieval and browser/Mac orchestration, not generation.
args.security_concerns: Commitment data is highly personal. Keep raw drafts and unrelated page text local where possible, send only normalized candidate facts and minimally necessary sources, and never transmit or submit revised wording without confirmation. Do not infer obligations from sensitive messages unless the owner has enabled that source.
missing: A commitment candidate extractor that works on draft text and spoken utterances without taking control of submission
A temporal feasibility evaluator that distinguishes hard conflicts from movable commitments and exposes its evidence
A low-disruption pendant warning channel with suppression during conversations or quiet hours
A confirmation-linked mutation path that can revise the originating draft and record before/after provenance

args.change: Add a dedicated, electrically hard-wired microphone privacy slider to the pendant with a visible red mechanical position and a firmware-readable state. The mute path should disconnect or gate the microphone before the application processor, emit a local click/LED confirmation, and include the mute state in every relay presence/status event. It must remain muted across reconnects and reboot until physically switched back.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can carry an always-listening device in meetings, at home, or around other people without having to trust software or remember a spoken command. They get an unmistakable physical guarantee that no audio is being captured.
args.effort: Medium hardware revision plus enclosure, PCB, firmware, and relay status handling; validate that boot, brownout, and reconnect paths cannot silently unmute.
args.risk: The switch could be bumped and cause missed commands, or its state could disagree with software. Fail safe toward muted, announce “microphone muted” locally, and show the state in the pendant LED and Mac dashboard. A self-test should detect switch/wiring disagreement.
args.cost_impact: Roughly $0.20–$1.00 in switch, PCB, and enclosure changes at prototype quantities; negligible steady-state power draw, with a small GPIO/input pull resistor cost.
args.latency_impact: No network latency; local mute takes effect electrically in milliseconds. Re-enabling capture may require a one-time handshake so the relay does not assume audio is available prematurely.
args.security_impact: Substantially reduces accidental audio exfiltration and gives the owner a trustworthy hardware boundary. The relay must treat missing or stale mute telemetry as unknown, never as unmuted.
depends_on: Pendant PCB/enclosure revision
Firmware boot and reconnect fail-closed behavior
Relay presence/status schema carrying microphone state
Dashboard and spoken-status handling for mute state

args.user_asks: “That’s not what I meant—fix the last thing you did.”
args.why_useful: Today an action receipt can tell the owner what happened, and some individual jobs can be undone, but a human correction often means “change the parameter” rather than simply reverse it. This gives the owner a spoken, cross-surface repair path: identify the referenced recent action, explain the proposed patch, and apply the smallest safe correction instead of forcing them to reconstruct the original workflow.
args.model_tier: Realtime for resolving the short spoken correction and selecting the recent receipt; a cheaper background model can compile and verify the patch. Execution remains deterministic on Mac/browser, with relay retaining the journal.
args.latency_budget: Acknowledge in under 1 second; show/speak the proposed repair within 5 seconds; execute reversible repairs within 15 seconds. Irreversible or ambiguous repairs stop for explicit confirmation.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.005–$0.03 per repair depending on whether semantic interpretation needs the realtime tier; most cost is receipt/context retrieval and any screenshot or page extraction, not deterministic execution.
args.security_concerns: Only recent owner-scoped receipts and the minimum related page/file context leave the device. Never infer authorization from the correction alone: sending, deleting, purchasing, or changing external records requires confirmation. Keep before/after values, tab URL, file path, and an undo token; redact secrets from the spoken response and dashboard.
missing: A durable cross-surface transaction journal that links Mac actions, browser mutations, and spoken intent under one repairable operation id
A semantic patch compiler that can turn “make it Tuesday instead” into a typed before/after change and reject unsupported repairs
A single confirmation/undo protocol shared by browser and Mac executors
Pendant delivery of a concise repair preview plus a local stop gesture

args.change: Create a cross-surface repair journal and semantic patch protocol. Every Mac/browser mutation and spoken request receives one operationId, stores typed before/after state plus provenance and an inverse or compensating action, and exposes PATCH /operations/:id/repair that accepts a constrained patch (field, old value, new value). The relay resolves “that last thing” to a candidate operation, the model may only fill the patch schema, and executors reject stale before-values or non-invertible actions. Return a preview and one-tap/pendant confirmation, then append the result as a new receipt.
args.why_useful_to_owner: When the assistant gets something slightly wrong, the owner can correct it naturally instead of manually undoing, reopening the right app, and repeating the whole task. Stale or dangerous changes fail visibly rather than silently overwriting newer work.
args.effort: Medium-high: shared operation schema and journal, adapters for existing Mac/browser receipts, patch validation, relay endpoint, and dashboard/pendant preview.
args.risk: Some actions have no safe inverse or external state may change; stale-value checks and confirmation are required. Recovery is to leave the original receipt untouched and provide a manual next step if repair is unsupported.
args.cost_impact: Negligible storage/compute; occasional low-cost model call for spoken correction. Screenshot/page extraction can dominate browser repairs.
args.latency_impact: Adds 1–3 seconds for candidate resolution and before-state validation; deterministic repairs remain within one job round trip.
args.security_impact: Improves auditability but centralizes sensitive before/after values. Encrypt journal fields, apply short retention, redact secrets, and enforce owner/job scoping.
depends_on: The existing receipt/undo implementation must expose stable operation IDs and typed before/after fields.
Browser command queue must return typed mutation receipts rather than only success/failure.
Owner confirmation and universal stop behavior must be wired into the shared executor.

args.change: Replace the prototype's 15.625 kHz I2S microphone plus ESP32 bridge audio split with a production audio path designed around native 24 kHz capture/playback: a low-power digital MEMS mic and codec/DSP feeding an MCU with at least 512 kB application RAM and hardware audio buffering, with the cellular modem isolated from the real-time audio task. Keep Opus at 24 kHz on uplink and downlink, and use a hardware sample-rate clock rather than the current 31.25 kHz wire-rate resampling workaround.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets clearer speech and fewer clipped or delayed replies, especially in noisy or musically rich environments. 24 kHz becomes a genuine end-to-end property rather than a 24 kHz decoder fed by narrower microphone audio.
args.effort: High: select a production SoC/audio codec, redesign board and power rails, update Zephyr drivers and Opus framing, and run acoustic plus radio coexistence tests. Preserve the dev-kit path behind a compile-time audio backend while the board is developed.
args.risk: New silicon, clocking, and RF layout can introduce noise or battery drain. Recovery is a dual-backend firmware build and an automatic fallback to the existing 16 kHz uplink when the native path fails self-test; never silently claim superwideband when capture is narrow.
args.cost_impact: Prototype BOM increase roughly $8–$20 for codec/mic/MCU and board changes, plus engineering NRE; likely 10–25% more audio power depending on DSP choice. API cost is unchanged, though 24 kHz Opus may use modestly more bandwidth.
args.latency_impact: Hardware buffering and modem isolation should reduce jitter; larger RAM enables 60 ms jitter buffering without starving the application. Initial codec buffering may add 5–15 ms.
args.security_impact: More audio remains in RAM buffers; keep buffers volatile, zero on stop, and retain the existing encrypted transport. A dedicated audio DSP must not gain access to secrets or application storage.
depends_on: Define and pass the audio acceptance test for native 24 kHz capture, 24 kHz Opus packets, decode, and speaker output.
Measure current battery and RF/audio coexistence baseline on the nRF9160 prototype.
Choose the production MCU and digital mic/codec before freezing PCB and enclosure.

args.user_asks: “I lost my pendant. Lock it now, keep my information safe, and let me continue from my Mac without losing my place.”
args.why_useful: A wearable is uniquely exposed to loss, theft, or being left in a room. Today continuity and revocation are separate infrastructure concerns: the owner cannot quickly invalidate the missing device while preserving legitimate work context. This makes loss a recoverable interruption rather than a privacy emergency and prevents an attacker holding the pendant from replaying queued audio, invoking actions, or learning private context.
args.model_tier: Realtime only for the owner's short loss report and immediate acknowledgement; deterministic relay security code performs revocation. A cheaper background model can assemble a redacted continuity packet on the Mac after the lock is complete.
args.latency_budget: Remote lock acknowledgement under 2 seconds when the relay is reachable; queued local lock takes effect on the pendant's next wake or button event. Mac continuity packet available within 30 seconds.
args.cost_estimate: Under $0.01 per incident; dominated by one authenticated relay request and optional local context summarization. No recurring model cost.
args.security_concerns: Revocation must require a second factor or an already-authenticated Mac session, otherwise anyone who hears the wake phrase could cause denial of service. Immediately invalidate device tokens, cancel pending audio/action deliveries, erase volatile audio and sensitive cache, quarantine queued jobs, and rotate session keys. Do not copy secrets into the continuity packet; show exactly what was retained and for how long. Require explicit confirmation before re-pairing a replacement pendant.
missing: A device identity and key lifecycle service with remote revoke, rotation, replacement pairing, and replay protection
A pendant firmware panic/revocation state that survives reboot and refuses cached commands offline
A relay-wide kill switch for pending audio, browser, and Mac jobs scoped to one device identity
A redacted continuity export that transfers only active task state to the authenticated Mac, with audit receipts and expiry

args.change: Add a persistent device-identity lifecycle to the pendant: hardware-backed device key, short-lived relay credentials, signed revocation epochs, and a local REVOKED mode stored in a tiny protected flash record. Every queued command and audio delivery must carry the device epoch; firmware rejects old epochs after reboot and zeroes volatile audio/context buffers on revocation. Replacement pairing requires a challenge approved from an authenticated Mac session plus a physical button gesture.
args.why_useful_to_owner: If the pendant is lost, the owner can make it harmless remotely without losing their active work, and a replacement can be paired without handing over their whole account. Stale queued commands cannot come alive later when the missing device reconnects.
args.effort: High firmware/relay/security work: key provisioning, epoch propagation through jobs and audio, protected flash handling, recovery UX, and adversarial testing for offline and replay cases.
args.risk: A false revocation or lost second factor could strand the owner. Provide a clearly documented recovery code stored outside the pendant and a Mac-only recovery flow; keep revocation idempotent and auditable.
args.cost_impact: Negligible per-request API cost; modest flash writes and roughly tens of bytes of protected state. Hardware-backed key support may add $1–$4 BOM if the chosen production MCU lacks a secure element.
args.latency_impact: One signature/epoch check per command, typically under milliseconds; remote lock remains relay-latency bound.
args.security_impact: Substantially reduces blast radius of pendant loss, but makes key provisioning and recovery high consequence. Never log private keys or recovery codes; rate-limit pairing and revoke all prior epochs on replacement.
depends_on: A relay device-identity registry and remote revocation endpoint.
Consistent device epoch fields in queued jobs, audio packets, and browser/Mac delivery receipts.
An authenticated Mac second-factor flow and owner-facing recovery-code storage.

args.user_asks: “Hold this for me until I have a quiet ten minutes.” The pendant should save what I said, have the relay and my Mac/browser gather only the relevant private context, and later give me a short cited audio packet with the decision or next step—without sending, submitting, or changing anything.
args.why_useful: This turns an interruption into progress instead of another forgotten note. The pendant is the only surface present at the interruption, the relay can keep the task alive, and the Mac/browser are the only places that can inspect private mail, calendar, files, and logged-in pages. It is deliberately preparation-only, so the owner gets value without an accidental commitment.
args.model_tier: Use gpt-realtime-2.1 only to capture/confirm the short handoff and play the final packet; use gpt-5.6-luna background jobs for evidence gathering and synthesis; use gpt-4.1-mini only for browser visual extraction if needed.
args.latency_budget: Acknowledge the handoff on the pendant in under 2 seconds; background evidence collection may take 1–5 minutes. Deliver at the next owner-selected quiet window, or queue it durably if every surface is offline.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.02–$0.10 per handoff depending on browser pages and synthesis; realtime audio and repeated private-page extraction dominate.
args.security_concerns: Private mail/calendar/browser content stays on the authenticated Mac/browser path and only a minimized, cited evidence packet crosses to the relay. Never send mail, submit forms, delete, buy, or create external commitments without a separate owner approval. Expire raw audio and page captures quickly; show sources and an undo/clear control in the dashboard.

an owner-controlled quiet-attention window and delivery acknowledgement queue
a cross-surface preflight/recovery path when the browser is offline or evidence becomes stale

args.change: Replace the provisional nRF9160-DK audio path with a product audio front end: a low-power stereo/mono 24 kHz-capable ADC/DAC (or dedicated audio DSP) connected over I2S to a cellular/application MCU, with DMA ring buffers and hardware clocking. Negotiate an explicit audio profile at session start: 24 kHz superwideband when battery/network/CPU budget permit, 16 kHz fallback otherwise. Keep Opus framing compatible at the relay boundary, but carry sample rate and profile in authenticated session metadata so the relay never silently resamples a supposedly 24 kHz call.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets genuinely clearer, more natural speech in both directions rather than a 15.625/16 kHz microphone being marketed as a 24 kHz path. The fallback preserves battery and call reliability when conditions are poor, while the explicit profile prevents confusing quality regressions.
args.effort: High: select codec/ADC, lay out and validate a new board, add Zephyr DMA/audio-clock drivers, tune Opus at 24 kHz under real cellular load, and add relay negotiation plus end-to-end waveform/latency tests.
args.risk: More BOM complexity, power draw, RF/audio interference, and firmware memory pressure. Recover with the existing dev-kit profile as a compatibility mode, watchdog the audio coprocessor, and fall back to 16 kHz on underrun or thermal/battery thresholds.
args.cost_impact: Approximately $3–$12 added BOM in low volume plus board redesign; roughly 20–80 mW additional audio-front-end draw depending on codec. API cost is unchanged; 24 kHz Opus may modestly increase bandwidth.
args.latency_impact: Potentially 10–30 ms lower buffering with DMA, but codec load can add processing time; negotiate a 60 ms or 20 ms frame profile and measure mouth-to-ear latency end to end.
args.security_impact: Authenticated profile negotiation and signed firmware are required; raw microphone audio remains transient and should not be retained on the device beyond ring buffers.
depends_on: End-to-end 24 kHz acceptance tests that inspect capture, relay transcode, decode, and speaker output rather than route labels
relay audio-profile negotiation and telemetry
a power/battery policy for selecting 24 kHz versus fallback
hardware prototype replacing the current nRF9160-DK assumptions

transcript.text:
Round 110 findings:

- Relay and Mac bridge are online, with durable audio and persistent state.
- Browser extension is offline with **10 pending commands**.
- Computer-use remains unavailable because Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions are still absent.
- The current pipeline is **not truly 24 kHz end to end**: observed microphone uplink is 15,625 Hz, while Mac TTS output is 24 kHz.

I added three proposals:

1. **“Hold this until I have ten quiet minutes”** — the pendant captures an interruption, the relay/Mac/browser gather relevant private context, and the owner later receives a short cited audio packet without any external action being taken.
2. **A real 24 kHz hardware/audio path** — dedicated audio hardware, explicit profile negotiation, and a measured fallback to 16 kHz when power or CPU requires it.
3. **Nightly synthetic audio conformance tests** — verify capture, relay, decoding, playback, clipping, underruns, and latency, and prohibit the system from claiming “24 kHz end to end” unless every leg passes.

What is still needed from the system is durable handoff linkage, attention-window scheduling, audio-profile negotiation, synthetic pendant diagnostics, and an end-to-end acceptance harness. What may still need owner action is reconnecting the browser extension and—if computer-use is desired—manually granting the two macOS TCC permissions.

args.user_asks: “Answer me privately; I’m in public.” The pendant should classify whether the reply contains sensitive information, keep private evidence on the Mac/browser, and deliver the answer through a private listening channel—or silently defer it—rather than speaking it aloud around other people.
args.why_useful: Today the owner must choose between getting useful assistance and exposing mail, calendar, health, finance, or work details to nearby people. This makes the pendant socially safe: it can still use the Mac and authenticated browser for rich answers, while the owner receives only an appropriately private rendering.
args.model_tier: Use the realtime model only for the live request and a short sensitivity decision; use the slower Mac planner for private-page retrieval and answer synthesis. A deterministic policy layer must override the model for secrets, authentication data, and owner-defined sensitive categories.
args.latency_budget: Acknowledge mode selection in under 500 ms and deliver a short answer in under 5 seconds when context is already available. If evidence gathering takes longer, provide a neutral private “working” cue and queue the result without speaking content aloud.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.01–$0.06 per request; private browser retrieval and synthesis dominate, not the sensitivity classifier.
args.security_concerns: Raw private page content must remain on the authenticated Mac/browser path; only the minimum answer crosses the relay. The device must never announce sensitive text while privacy mode is uncertain. Require a physical mode confirmation for ambiguous cases, provide a hard local mute/stop control, and log only policy decisions rather than spoken content.
missing: A product pendant with a genuinely private output path (bone-conduction, near-ear speaker, or encrypted paired earbud) and a local proximity/wear-state sensor
an authenticated sensitivity-policy evaluator with owner-editable categories and a fail-closed default
an end-to-end delivery acknowledgement that distinguishes privately heard, deferred, and accidentally audible
relay and Mac routing that keeps citations/evidence off the spoken/public channel while retaining them in the dashboard

args.change: Design the wearable around a privacy-capable output path instead of the current open playback assumption: add a near-ear bone-conduction or sealed directional transducer, a skin-contact/wear sensor, a hardware mute switch, and a secure audio-profile handshake to the relay. The firmware must refuse spoken playback when the device is not worn or the private channel is not confirmed, while retaining the existing open speaker only for explicitly non-sensitive responses.
args.why_useful_to_owner: They can use the assistant in meetings, transit, cafés, and shared homes without broadcasting private information. A physical mute and fail-closed wear check make privacy dependable even when the network or model is wrong.
args.effort: High: industrial design, acoustic and RF coexistence testing, power budgeting, secure accessory pairing, new firmware drivers, and relay policy integration.
args.risk: Bone conduction can be uncomfortable or hard to hear in loud environments; the sealed path may increase heat and battery use. Recover with an explicit open-audio fallback only after a physical button confirmation, plus local volume and mute controls.
args.cost_impact: Approximately $8–$25 incremental low-volume BOM and 30–150 mW additional draw depending on transducer and amplifier; no material per-call API cost.
args.latency_impact: Negligible signal latency, though pairing and wear-state confirmation may add 100–300 ms before playback.

args.user_asks: “Read me the brief. If I say ‘why?’, show me the source and let me open it on my Mac.”
args.why_useful: A spoken summary is otherwise a dead end: the owner can hear that something changed but cannot quickly judge whether it is real or act on it. Each audio item would carry a compact provenance token (source, capture time, freshness, confidence, and the exact supporting excerpt). Saying “why?” on the pendant retrieves the evidence, while “open it” uses the authenticated browser or Mac to reveal the original page without requiring the owner to remember which tab produced it. This is a genuinely joined behavior: the pendant supplies low-friction speech and playback, relay preserves the item identity, faculty-perception checks freshness, browser holds private sessions, and Mac presents the evidence.
args.model_tier: Realtime only for the short spoken answer and disambiguation; background extraction, excerpt hashing, freshness checks, and briefing assembly use a cheaper background model. No model call for a direct cached-source lookup.
args.latency_budget: Initial “why?” response under 2 seconds from cached provenance; source opening under 5 seconds when the browser bridge is online. If the bridge is offline, speak the citation and queue the open request rather than claiming it opened.
args.cost_estimate: Typically one small realtime turn for the spoken explanation; background extraction dominates but can use a cheap model. Direct provenance lookup is near-zero model cost. Browser/Mac execution cost is local/API latency, not inference.
args.security_concerns: Private URLs, excerpts, and account names must remain scoped to the authenticated owner and never enter generic logs or model context unless needed. Opening a source is reversible navigation, but any follow-up mutation remains gated by the existing confirmation policy. Never report a source as opened without a verified browser/Mac receipt; stale or conflicting evidence must be spoken as such.
missing: A stable briefing-item schema and provenance token that survives audio encoding, queueing, interruption, and reconnect
A read-only provenance lookup route returning source, excerpt hash, freshness, and confidence
A pendant utterance intent for why/source/open plus a resumable audio-item cursor
A browser/Mac verified-open operation with explicit offline/blocked outcome
A policy deciding which excerpt and URL fields may be spoken aloud

args.user_asks: “When your sources disagree, don’t guess. Tell me what conflicts, ask the one question that resolves it, and remember the answer for next time.”
args.why_useful: The owner currently gets plausible but unsafe answers when machine context, cached briefings, browser state, and remembered preferences disagree. This turns uncertainty into a tiny, actionable interaction: the pendant says the conflict in one sentence, asks only the minimum disambiguating question, and the relay records the owner’s answer with scope, source, and expiry. Future agents then stop re-opening the same ambiguity (for example, the authoritative timezone) and can explain which evidence they used.
args.model_tier: Realtime for stating the conflict and asking the one question; background model only for clustering repeated conflicts and suggesting a candidate resolution. Deterministic source comparison handles ordinary timestamps, reachability, and receipt states.
args.latency_budget: Conflict detection should add less than 300 ms to an answer when evidence is already present. The owner’s clarification is one short turn. Persist the resolution immediately; no Mac/browser round trip is required unless they are the conflicting source.
args.cost_estimate: Near-zero for deterministic conflicts; one short realtime turn only when clarification is required. Background clustering is infrequent and cheap.
args.security_concerns: Never expose secret values while explaining a conflict; say “a saved private fact” rather than reading it. Store only the owner-approved resolution, its scope, provenance, and expiry. Do not silently overwrite a higher-authority fact; retain both claims and mark one superseded. Time-sensitive actions must remain blocked until resolution.
missing: A conflict object schema (claims, authorities, timestamps, scope, confidence, safe redaction)
A deterministic resolver that compares machine-context, browser, briefing, receipt, and memory evidence before model narration
A one-question clarification policy and owner answer route
Durable supersession/expiry semantics in the shared context projection
A pendant-visible acknowledgement that the resolution was saved

args.change: Replace the prototype’s single multifunction button/LED with a dedicated, physically latched microphone mute switch plus a high-visibility two-color privacy LED, and expose its state as a signed device event. The relay must treat mute as an absolute input gate: stop capture, cancel pending speech transmission, mark queued work as locally muted, and tell Mac/browser surfaces not to start new capture or automation that depends on live speech until an explicit unmute event.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can know, by touch and sight, that the pendant is not listening—especially in a meeting or around other people—without trusting a spoken claim from the same software being muted. The state follows the job across relay, Mac, and browser, preventing a stale queued command from surprising them after privacy mode is enabled.
args.effort: Moderate hardware revision and firmware/pipeline integration: GPIO debouncing, LED state machine, signed mute/unmute events, relay enforcement, and tests for disconnect/reconnect and queued audio. No industrial design can be finalized until the pendant moves beyond the nRF9160 DK prototype.
args.risk: A stuck switch or brownout could leave the owner muted; provide a clear LED fault pattern and a button-held recovery/self-test. If the event link is down, local mute still works and unmute should fail closed for capture until state is acknowledged. Do not infer privacy from network reachability.
args.cost_impact: One latching switch, LED/light-pipe, resistor, and small PCB change, roughly $1–$4 in BOM at volume; negligible power compared with the modem and audio path. No per-invocation API cost.
args.latency_impact: Local mute cutoff should be under one audio frame (<60 ms); relay propagation is best-effort and should not delay local privacy.
args.security_impact: Improves privacy materially: mute state is hardware-originated, authenticated, and fail-closed. Avoid logging raw audio or secret event payloads; retain only state transitions and timestamps.
depends_on: A signed pendant event envelope and reconnect state reconciliation
Relay enforcement that distinguishes hardware mute from software pause
Cross-surface cancellation of queued audio and speech-dependent jobs
A product pendant revision beyond the current nRF9160 development kit

args.user_asks: “Why did we decide that? Reconstruct the short chain of evidence, assumptions, and approvals that led to it, and tell me what has changed since.”
args.why_useful: Today the system can perform pieces of research, planning, and execution, but the owner cannot later audit a consequential personal or work decision as a coherent story. This capability would let them recover the actual decision context: what the pendant heard, which private page or Mac document supplied evidence, what was uncertain, what the owner approved, and which later facts invalidate the conclusion. It is not an action-history list; it is a time-bounded, evidence-linked explanation of a decision and its present validity.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic event/provenance joins first; use the cheaper background model to summarize the chain. Reserve realtime for the owner’s spoken question and a concise answer, with drill-down only on request.
args.latency_budget: A cached decision packet should yield a spoken answer in under 3 seconds; reconstructing missing links may take up to 20 seconds and must be labeled incomplete rather than silently inferred.
args.cost_estimate: Low per query when event joins and hashes are available; occasional background summarization dominates. No need to resend full page contents or audio—store compact excerpts/hashes and retrieve originals only when authorized.
args.security_concerns: Decision chains may expose private mail, documents, or health/work context. Enforce per-source access at replay time, redact secrets and unrelated people, preserve immutable provenance, and distinguish owner approval from model suggestion. Never claim an approval that lacks a recorded owner event.
missing: A durable decision entity with links to claims, source snapshots, model suggestions, owner approvals, and resulting actions
Immutable, privacy-filtered event snapshots for browser pages, Mac files, pendant utterances, and action receipts
A change detector that compares the original evidence against current accessible sources and reports invalidation
A spoken drill-down protocol that keeps the owner on one decision while fetching a specific source or receipt
Retention and deletion controls that can erase a decision chain without leaving orphaned sensitive artifacts

args.user_asks: “Forget everything about that topic everywhere.”
args.why_useful: The owner should be able to revoke a sensitive conversation as a single intent, rather than hunting through pendant audio, relay jobs, browser extracts, Mac drafts, and derived memory. The system would first enumerate what it found, then delete or cryptographically tombstone the source recordings, derived summaries, queued jobs, browser snapshots, and local notes across reachable surfaces, reporting any unreachable residue and retrying later. This is a real cross-surface privacy power that does not exist today.
args.model_tier: Realtime only to identify the topic and confirm scope; deterministic entity matching and deletion orchestration should run in the background. Use a cheap model only to resolve ambiguous references, never to decide deletion scope silently.
args.latency_budget: Show a deletion plan within 3 seconds from indexed records; complete reachable deletion within 30 seconds, with durable retries for offline Mac/browser and a concise receipt when finished.
args.cost_estimate: Low model cost; storage/index scans and Mac/browser round trips dominate. Cost grows with the number of artifacts, not conversation length.
args.security_concerns: This is destructive and must require explicit confirmation unless the owner has separately enabled a narrow auto-delete rule. Never delete unrelated records from a fuzzy topic match. Keep a minimal non-content tombstone (identifier, scope, time, completion state) so the system can prove what was removed, while allowing the owner to erase even that audit marker under a stronger confirmation.
missing: A cross-surface artifact index linking raw audio, transcripts, summaries, context facts, browser snapshots, Mac files, and queued jobs
A deletion planner with exact-match/ambiguous-match classification and owner confirmation
Idempotent delete/tombstone APIs for relay storage, browser sessions, and Mac workspace artifacts
Offline retry leases and a verified deletion receipt that distinguishes deleted, unreachable, and not-found
A pendant intent and local pre-transmission cancellation path for newly captured audio

transcript.text:
Recorded two capabilities:

1. **Decision replay:** Ask, “Why did we decide that?” and receive a provenance-linked explanation of the evidence, assumptions, approvals, and what has changed since.
2. **Cross-surface forgetting:** Say, “Forget everything about that topic everywhere,” and have the system identify and delete related audio, transcripts, summaries, browser snapshots, Mac files, queued jobs, and derived memory—with a verified receipt showing what was deleted or unreachable.

They require durable cross-surface provenance, artifact indexing, scoped deletion orchestration, offline retry leases, and explicit confirmation for destructive erasure.

args.user_asks: “Tell me when my commitments conflict, and give me the least-painful way out.”
args.why_useful: Instead of separate reminders and briefs, the system would notice that a calendar promise, an email deadline, a travel reservation, or a logged-in task now makes another promise impossible. It would show the evidence and propose concrete options (move, delegate, decline, or ask for an extension), drafting messages but never sending them. The pendant can ask one short clarification at the moment a choice is needed; the Mac and browser do the evidence gathering that the pendant cannot.
args.model_tier: Background/slow model builds a normalized obligation and conflict graph from Calendar, Mail, local notes/files, and authenticated browser pages; realtime model is used only to explain one conflict and collect a choice through the pendant. Deterministic rules handle overlap, travel-time, due-date, and dependency checks before any model judgment.
args.latency_budget: Nightly and event-triggered scans may take 1–5 minutes. A newly detected high-confidence conflict should produce a queued capsule, not an interruption; once the owner asks, the first evidence-backed answer should be under 3 seconds. Draft generation may take up to 20 seconds.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.02–$0.15 per daily scan depending on how many private pages and messages are extracted; most cost is summarization and reconciliation, not rule checks. One realtime clarification is a normal short turn.
args.security_concerns: Private mail, calendar, files, and authenticated pages leave their surfaces only as bounded extracts with source, timestamp, and sensitivity labels. Never send, cancel, reschedule, purchase, or disclose without explicit confirmation. Conflicts involving secrets or health/financial data should be redacted in spoken output and linked to a Mac review workbench.
missing: A durable obligation schema with source citations, confidence, due/temporal constraints, and expiry
A conflict detector that distinguishes true impossibility from merely adjacent events and accounts for travel/buffer time
A ranked option generator with reversible draft artifacts and an explicit approval boundary
Event hooks from Calendar/Mail/browser watches into the detector, plus deduplication and quiet-hour delivery

args.change: Create a durable obligation-and-conflict event layer between existing context graph/research/briefing routes: normalize commitments from Calendar, Mail, local notes, and authenticated browser extracts into typed obligations; emit idempotent conflict events with source citations, temporal/travel constraints, confidence, expiry, and a ranked set of reversible options. Persist a draft-only resolution packet that the Mac workbench and pendant queue can consume, with explicit owner approval required for any external mutation.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets an early, explainable warning that two promises cannot both be kept, plus a ready way out, rather than discovering the collision during a meeting or after a deadline. It turns existing disconnected reads and briefs into dependable life coordination.
args.effort: Medium-high: schema and D1/R2 persistence, Calendar/Mail/notes/browser adapters, deterministic temporal rules, conflict deduplication, and a review/approval packet rendered by Mac and pendant. Start with calendar + browser deadlines, then add mail and local files.
args.risk: False conflicts could create alert fatigue; mitigate with confidence thresholds, quiet-hour queueing, evidence links, and a dismiss/merge feedback loop. Never execute a cancellation, send, or reschedule from the detector. If a source is unavailable, mark the conflict incomplete rather than infer absence.
args.cost_impact: Low recurring storage and rule-evaluation cost; background model extraction is the dominant API cost, approximately cents per scan. No new hardware required.
args.latency_impact: Event ingestion is near-real-time where hooks exist; reconciliation is seconds to minutes. Spoken delivery waits for a stable packet and should remain under 3 seconds after it is queued.
args.security_impact: Sensitive source text stays bounded and provenance-tagged; spoken output uses redacted summaries. Approval packets must preserve the exact before/after effect and source evidence, and expired source extracts must be deleted on the retention policy.
depends_on: Durable typed context projection rather than hand-written fleetContext
Authenticated browser command/session reliability and truthful offline status
A durable review queue with acknowledgment, expiry, and approval gates
Calendar/Mail event or polling adapters on the Mac agent

args.user_asks: “Learn how I like things handled, but ask before you make a new rule.”
args.why_useful: The owner repeatedly says the same things—never send without approval, keep spoken replies short, defer low-urgency items, prefer reminders over email—but today those choices are scattered across pendant turns, Mac receipts, browser approvals, and dismissed briefings. The hive would infer a candidate personal operating rule from repeated behavior, show three concrete examples, and let the owner accept, edit, or reject it. Accepted rules would then make every surface less annoying without silently changing autonomy boundaries.
args.model_tier: A cheap background model clusters decisions and dismissals; deterministic counters and policy constraints prevent overgeneralization. Realtime is used only when presenting a candidate rule or answering 'why did you do that?'.
args.latency_budget: Learnings can be computed nightly or after 10 relevant events. Candidate presentation should be a 20–30 second spoken interaction, with a Mac review page for details. Applying an accepted rule is immediate and must be reflected in the next task.
args.cost_estimate: Usually under $0.01 per nightly update; dominant cost is embedding/clustering a small decision history. No model call is needed for every action.
args.security_concerns: Behavioral history is highly personal. Store derived rules separately from raw transcripts, retain source references with short TTLs, and never infer sensitive traits or rules about health, relationships, or money. A candidate cannot widen permissions or authorize irreversible actions; owner confirmation is mandatory and revocation must be one utterance.
missing: A versioned preference/policy registry with scope (surface/task), confidence, examples, expiry, and revocation
A decision-outcome event stream covering pendant acknowledgments, Mac receipts, browser approvals, and briefing dismissals
A conservative rule learner that distinguishes stable preference from one-off context
A spoken-plus-Mac review and rollback UI with exact before/after behavior simulation

I also identified the concrete integration layer missing between existing context-graph, research, briefing, capture, browser, and job-receipt primitives.

args.user_asks: “Help me negotiate this without committing me to anything.”
args.why_useful: For an incoming request, bill, offer, scheduling demand, or support dispute, the owner would get a private negotiation packet: what the other party is asking, what the owner has already promised, hard constraints from calendar and account data, plausible concessions, a recommended position, and a ready-to-edit reply. The pendant can ask one focused question about the owner's priority; the Mac and authenticated browser can gather the surrounding evidence. Nothing is sent or accepted until the owner approves the exact wording and commitment.
args.model_tier: A background model extracts the request and generates alternatives from cited evidence; deterministic checks identify existing commitments and monetary/date changes. Realtime is reserved for the short clarification and spoken summary, not packet construction.
args.latency_budget: A packet from already-open sources should be ready in 30–90 seconds; broader research may take several minutes. Spoken clarification should be under 2 seconds after the packet is available.
args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.03–$0.25 per packet, dominated by reading private pages/threads and generating alternatives; deterministic constraint checks are negligible.
args.security_concerns: The packet may contain private correspondence, account details, and negotiation strategy. Keep raw source material on its owning surface where possible, transfer only bounded excerpts with provenance, redact secrets in voice, and require explicit confirmation for every outbound message, acceptance, payment, cancellation, or changed promise. Never infer a reservation price or disclose one without the owner's statement.
missing: A negotiation-specific packet schema for asks, constraints, concessions, authority, and commitments
Cross-surface extraction of the relevant thread/page plus the owner's existing commitments with stable citations
A consequence simulator that shows what each proposed reply would commit the owner to
A review UI and pendant interaction that supports edit, reject, or approve-exactly-this-text, with no implicit send

args.change: Add a negotiation-packet compiler and consequence simulator that accepts a cited incoming request from Mail/browser, resolves only the owner's relevant calendar/account commitments, and produces three explicitly labeled reply variants (accept, counter, decline). For each variant, compute the exact new date, money, access, or communication commitments it would create, show source evidence and unresolved assumptions, and emit an immutable approval token tied to the exact text. Outbound adapters must reject any send or submit lacking that token.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can respond confidently to difficult requests without manually reconstructing context or accidentally agreeing to something hidden in a polished draft. They see the consequences before committing and can approve only the exact reply they intend.
args.effort: Medium: packet schema, evidence joiner, deterministic consequence rules, text/version hashing, and adapters for Mac Mail and authenticated browser forms; a Mac review surface and pendant summary are needed.
args.risk: The model may miss an obligation or misread leverage; expose uncertainty and source excerpts, offer no-answer/ask-for-time variants, and fail closed when evidence is incomplete. Version hashes prevent a later edit from being sent under an earlier approval.
args.cost_impact: Small persistent storage and hashing cost; roughly cents per packet for extraction and alternatives, with no recurring cost after approval.
args.latency_impact: Compilation takes tens of seconds for local sources and minutes for multiple private tabs; exact-text approval and send can be immediate once the packet is ready.
args.security_impact: Sensitive negotiations stay scoped to the selected thread and sources, with redacted voice summaries and short-lived packet retention. Approval tokens are single-use, audience-bound, and cannot authorize unrelated actions.
depends_on: A stable cross-surface source citation format
Draft-only Mac Mail and browser form adapters
Durable versioned approval records and truthful send receipts
Owner-configurable retention and disclosure boundaries

On a pendant interruption, create one handoffId with the raw intent reference, normalized goal, constraints, uncertainty, stopping point, owner timezone/quiet hours, and expiry. args.user_asks: “Before you use my Mac or logged-in browser for this, tell me exactly what private information would leave my devices, remove anything unnecessary, and let me approve the smallest safe version.”
args.why_useful: The owner can currently approve an action, but not inspect or constrain the information flow that makes it possible. This gives them a practical privacy boundary across the hive: the pendant states the proposed data footprint in one short sentence, the Mac/browser perform local minimization, and the relay records only a redacted proof of what was shared. It is different from an action receipt or an irreversible-action confirmation: the decision is about disclosure before research or execution begins, including disclosures to the model itself.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic classifiers and field-level redaction for known secrets, contacts, tokens, and private-page regions. Use a cheaper background model to explain the remaining data footprint. Use realtime only for the short spoken disclosure summary and the owner’s approve/edit/deny response.
args.latency_budget: For ordinary requests, compute a disclosure preview in under 2 seconds and speak it in one sentence. If classification is incomplete, pause and label the unknown rather than silently transmitting. Redaction can add seconds to a browser or Mac job, but must happen before any model or remote service receives the content.
args.cost_estimate: Usually under $0.01 per request for local deterministic scanning; $0.01–$0.05 when an explanation model is needed. The dominant cost is not the scan but any subsequent browser/Mac extraction, which should be reduced by sending minimized excerpts instead of full pages.
args.security_concerns: This is itself security-sensitive: the preview must be generated locally where possible and must not echo secrets into relay logs or pendant audio. Maintain an append-only disclosure manifest with hashes, categories, destination, and approval—not raw data. Require fresh approval if the destination, data category, target account, or action hash changes. Deny by default when a token, password, financial identifier, or unrelated person’s private content cannot be reliably removed.
missing: A preflight data-flow manifest spanning relay, model, Mac, and browser boundaries, with field-level redaction and destination labels.
Local secret/PII classification on the Mac and browser extension, plus a way to return redacted excerpts and proof hashes rather than raw captures.
A disclosure approval token separate from action approval, bound to the exact minimized payload and destination.
Dashboard and pendant rendering for a compact privacy preview, including an explicit unknown/blocked state.

args.change: Insert a Disclosure Preflight stage before /plan, browser extraction, model invocation, or /execute. It should build a typed manifest of every proposed input and destination (pendant, relay, model tier, Mac app, browser origin, external recipient), run local redaction on the Mac/extension, replace raw values with minimized excerpts or salted proof hashes, and issue a single-use disclosure token bound to the exact payload hash, destination set, and expiry. Downstream routes must reject requests without a matching token; any changed tab, target, field, or model destination invalidates it. Store only the manifest and approval decision in receipts, never the unredacted payload.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets a real, enforceable boundary instead of a reassuring prompt: private account pages, unrelated messages, credentials, and personal files cannot silently become model context just because a task crossed surfaces. They can approve a useful minimized request without choosing between total automation and total refusal.
args.effort: High: define the manifest schema, implement local scanners/redactors in the Mac and browser bridge, enforce token checks in relay routes, add safe failure behavior, and add compact pendant/dashboard rendering. Start with known credential/PII classes and expand classifiers after telemetry proves low false-negative rates.
args.risk: Over-redaction can make tasks fail or produce misleading results; under-redaction is a privacy breach. Fail closed for secrets and unknown destinations, show what was omitted, and allow the owner to explicitly widen scope by category—not by blindly forwarding the original page. Recovery is to re-run preflight after edits; never fall back to raw capture.
args.cost_impact: Low per-request compute for local scanning; modest storage for manifests and hashes. It may reduce model token cost by shrinking context, while adding engineering and maintenance cost for classifiers.
args.latency_impact: Adds roughly 0.5–2 seconds for local preflight; remote/model work starts only after approval. Cached classification for unchanged pages can make repeat requests near-instant.
args.security_impact: Strongly improves least-privilege and auditability, but the classifier and token verifier become security-critical. Keep manifests redacted, isolate keys, rotate token signing keys, and ensure logs cannot reconstruct sensitive values.
depends_on: A shared typed cross-surface payload manifest and destination taxonomy
Mac/browser local redaction and proof-hash services
Relay enforcement of scoped disclosure tokens
Owner-visible privacy preview and approval UI/audio

args.user_asks: “Keep track of the things I promise people—including things I say casually—and, at the right time, remind me with the context I need; let me mark it done or prepare the follow-up without sending anything.”
args.why_useful: People lose commitments between a spoken aside, a calendar event, an email thread, and a private web task. The pendant can catch the promise at the moment it is made; the relay can preserve it when the Mac is asleep; the Mac and authenticated browser can later find supporting context and verify completion. This is a closed loop rather than another reminder: it distinguishes a promise from a thought, asks only when ambiguity matters, and gives a sourced next action without silently contacting anyone.
args.model_tier: Use the realtime tier only to detect/clarify a commitment during conversation. Use a cheaper background model for nightly reconciliation, evidence extraction, deadline prediction, and drafting. Keep pendant-side capture deterministic and offline-capable.
args.latency_budget: Capture acknowledgement under 500 ms locally/relay-side; no blocking lookup during conversation. Reconciliation can run in 1–5 minutes after connectivity and a quiet-hours-aware check-in can arrive at the next useful moment.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.01–$0.05 per commitment lifecycle, dominated by background synthesis and authenticated-page extraction; most spoken acknowledgements should avoid a model call. Storage is small text plus provenance; browser screenshots should be opt-in and short-lived.
args.security_concerns: Commitments may contain sensitive names, health, or work data. Store a redacted commitment and encrypted provenance, with per-source sensitivity and TTL. Reading logged-in mail/browser pages is allowed by the owner's policy, but sending mail, submitting forms, deleting data, or changing a calendar item requires explicit approval. Every reminder should show why it believes the commitment is open and which evidence it used.
missing: A durable commitment/obligation ledger with tentative versus confirmed state, owner-visible provenance, due-window and recurrence fields, deduplication, and completion/snooze semantics.
A cross-surface reconciliation worker that can join pendant utterances to Calendar/Mail/Notes/browser evidence without copying whole pages into prompts.
A local interruption gate and pendant delivery acknowledgement so a reminder is deferred safely when the owner is driving, speaking, or offline.
An approval-aware action compiler that turns a confirmed follow-up into a previewable draft and receipt.

args.change: Replace the prototype’s 15,625 Hz I2S microphone/clock path with a production audio front end that captures 24 kHz (preferably a 48 kHz digital MEMS mic plus deterministic decimation, or a native 24 kHz I2S clock), and carry an explicit audio-format contract through firmware, relay transcoding, and Mac playback. Keep 24 kHz Opus decode on playback, but stop advertising the path as superwideband when uplink capture is physically limited to 15,625 Hz. Add an end-to-end test fixture that records a swept 8–12 kHz signal and verifies sample rate, timestamps, packet loss concealment, and intelligibility at the pendant.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets genuinely clearer speech and more reliable recognition of names and consonants in noisy everyday use, rather than a 24 kHz label applied to narrowband input. It also makes the wearable’s answer sound consistent in both directions and exposes failures before they become confusing conversations.
args.effort: High: select and layout a mic/clock, update nRF9160 I2S/DMA and Opus framing, update relay resampling/metadata, and run acoustic plus LTE-M power validation. Treat the current Nordic DK as a bring-up fixture, not the final enclosure.
args.risk: A clock/DMA mismatch can produce drift, buffer overruns, or dropped packets; higher-rate capture may expose the already-heavy CPU budget (encode ~15 ms per call and encode+decode about 87% of one core). Roll out behind a negotiated format bit and retain the current 16 kHz uplink fallback. If LTE-M power or CPU is unacceptable, capture at 48 kHz locally but downsample to a verified 24 kHz frame before encoding.
args.cost_impact: Roughly $3–$15 incremental BOM for a better digital mic/clock and power regulation in volume (more for a redesigned board); modest additional LTE-M airtime and RAM/DMA buffers, plus engineering/test cost. API cost is unchanged if transcoding stays deterministic.
args.latency_impact: Potentially +5–15 ms for resampling and larger buffers; preserve 60 ms Opus framing and negotiate down to 16 kHz on weak links.
args.security_impact: No new data class, but higher-fidelity audio can reveal more ambient detail. Keep existing transport encryption, avoid retaining raw PCM, and make format negotiation and recording retention observable in receipts.

Relay and Mac playback updates that reject mislabeled sample rates instead of silently resampling twice

transcript.text:
This round produced two proposals:

1. **Commitment loop:** The pendant captures casual promises, the relay preserves them across disconnections, and the Mac/browser later reconcile them with calendar, mail, notes, and private web pages. At the right time, the pendant gives a sourced reminder and can prepare—but never silently send—the follow-up.

2. **Honest 24 kHz audio path:** The current microphone captures at 15,625 Hz, so the system cannot truthfully call uplink audio superwideband. A production audio front end, explicit format negotiation, end-to-end sample-rate tests, and a verified 16 kHz fallback are needed.

What I still need is not another permission request. The important missing infrastructure is:

- A durable commitment/obligation ledger with provenance, due windows, deduplication, completion, and snooze states.
- Cross-surface reconciliation that can join a spoken commitment to calendar, mail, notes, and authenticated browser evidence without copying whole pages into prompts.
- A local interruption gate and delivery acknowledgement so reminders defer safely when the owner is busy, driving, offline, or already speaking.
- An approval-aware follow-up compiler producing previews, evidence, and receipts.
- A verified 24 kHz audio acceptance test plus CPU, RAM, LTE-M power, and playback measurements on the actual target wearable.

The Mac’s Accessibility/Screen Recording and browser-bridge grants remain owner-side blockers; I will not re-request them. The accessibility-free AppleScript, relay, pendant, and authenticated-read surfaces are sufficient to build the commitment loop’s first version.

args.user_asks: “When I leave home, work, or another place I choose, quietly check where I’m going next and tell me what I need to bring, finish, or remember before I get there.”
args.why_useful: A calendar reminder says where an appointment is; it does not notice that the owner is actually leaving, reconcile the destination with open work and private web tasks, or catch the one item left behind. The pendant can provide the moment-of-departure signal, the relay can remain available when the Mac sleeps, and the Mac/browser can assemble a short, evidence-backed departure checklist from calendar, mail, notes, and logged-in reservation or work pages. This is proactive physical-world context, not another scheduled briefing.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic geofence and calendar matching first. Use a cheaper background model to compose and rank the checklist. Reserve realtime only for ambiguous spoken corrections such as “I’m not going to the office after all.”
args.latency_budget: A departure event should produce a useful checklist within 5–15 seconds, with a local fallback such as “You have an appointment nearby.” Background page reconciliation may take up to two minutes and must never delay leaving.
args.cost_estimate: Usually below $0.01 per departure when calendar and cached context suffice; $0.02–$0.08 when authenticated browser extraction or synthesis is needed. GNSS checks and LTE-M bursts add battery cost, so use motion-triggered sampling and coarse geofences rather than continuous tracking.
args.security_concerns: Location history is highly sensitive. Keep exact coordinates on-device, send only a named place and coarse destination when possible, expire departure events quickly, and provide a hardware-button or voice disable mode. Browser/mail content must remain source-scoped and cited. Never send a message, alter a reservation, or buy anything from the checklist without explicit confirmation.
missing: Pendant-side GNSS/geofence and motion-trigger support, with coarse-place derivation that works during a dropped LTE link.
A privacy-preserving place profile store: named places, entry/exit rules, retention limits, and an owner-visible audit trail.
A destination resolver that joins place events to calendar and relevant open threads, then ranks only time-critical checklist items.
A local checklist cache and delivery acknowledgement so the pendant can speak a short fallback even when the Mac, browser bridge, or relay is unavailable.
built_from: POST /pipeline/events for departure and delivery provenance
POST /capture and GET /capture for owner corrections and one-off place notes
GET /machine-context and GET /context-graph for current destination and relevant entities
GET /briefing/latest and POST /briefing for the spoken checklist queue
POST /routines and POST /routines/:routineId/run for geofence-triggered reconciliation
GET /browser/sessions and the authenticated browser inspection/command-result routes for private reservation and work context
POST /execute and GET /jobs/:jobId/receipts for any explicitly approved follow-up action

args.change: Add a local departure-signal subsystem to the wearable: GNSS-capable location sampling with geofence evaluation and a low-power motion trigger, keeping exact coordinates in volatile/on-device storage and emitting only a named/coarse place-transition event upstream. Include a physical privacy-disable gesture and a bounded local checklist cache for disconnected operation.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can receive a timely, private “before you leave” checklist without carrying the phone or remembering to ask. It catches forgotten items and preparation steps at the only moment they are still fixable, while avoiding a permanent location trail in the cloud.
args.effort: High: select or enable GNSS on the nRF9160 design, characterize acquisition and LTE-M coexistence, implement geofence/motion firmware, privacy controls, encrypted local state, and relay event semantics. Product enclosure and antenna redesign may be required.
args.risk: GNSS can be slow indoors, inaccurate in cities, and power-hungry; false departures could annoy the owner. Use hysteresis, motion confirmation, named-place confidence, quiet hours, and a local disable latch. If GNSS is unavailable, fall back to owner-triggered place changes and never claim certainty.
args.cost_impact: Approximately $2–$10 incremental BOM if the modem/antenna can be reused, potentially more for RF and enclosure redesign. GNSS acquisition adds intermittent power draw and may increase LTE-M airtime only when a place transition is confirmed.
args.latency_impact: Cold fixes may take tens of seconds, so motion-triggered prediction and cached geofences should provide an immediate provisional event; final confirmation can arrive later. No impact on ordinary voice latency.
args.security_impact: Materially increases the sensitivity of the device. Exact coordinates must not leave the pendant by default; retain only coarse place IDs and short-lived transition records upstream. Privacy disable must be locally enforceable even with a compromised relay.
depends_on: A typed place-transition event contract shared by pendant, relay, Mac, and dashboard
A durable privacy policy for location retention and source disclosure
A local checklist cache and delivery acknowledgement protocol
A destination/context joiner that consumes the coarse event without requiring raw coordinates

args.user_asks: Keep my pendant useful all day: when its battery or connection is getting weak, quietly move non-urgent work to my Mac or the relay, save anything needed for later, and only interrupt me if I must act before the device goes offline.
args.why_useful: The pendant is the one surface that follows the owner, but it cannot be the only place work lives. This would preserve briefings, queued requests, and follow-ups through battery drain, Wi‑Fi loss, or leaving the Mac behind—without making the owner micromanage which machine is awake.
args.model_tier: Use a cheap background model for forecasting battery/connection risk and classifying urgency; use realtime only for the spoken warning or owner conversation. The Mac/relay should execute deterministic migration and checkpoint logic without an LLM where possible.
args.latency_budget: Health scoring every 1–5 minutes; migration/checkpoint within 10 seconds of a threshold; spoken warning under 1 second once a genuinely time-sensitive item is identified. No warning for routine degradation.
args.cost_estimate: Near-zero model cost for deterministic telemetry and queue migration; occasional small background-model calls for urgency classification (sub-cent scale). Main cost is durable queue/checkpoint storage and a few relay wakeups.
args.security_concerns: Battery, network, and queued-work metadata leave the pendant only to the authenticated relay/Mac; page contents and secrets must not be copied merely because a migration occurs. Require confirmation before migrating an irreversible action or sending anything; preserve owner-visible receipts and allow cancellation.
missing: Pendant battery/link telemetry exposed to the relay with hysteresis and last-known timestamp
A portable, resumable job checkpoint format with leases and deduplication across relay and Mac
Urgency/deadline metadata on queued work and a policy that distinguishes safe background migration from owner approval
A reconnect handoff protocol that lets the pendant retrieve a compact spoken summary and pending actions after an outage

args.change: Add an energy-and-link-aware work lease coordinator between pendant, relay, and Mac. It polls authenticated health/ops telemetry, assigns every queued job a deadline, reversibility, required surface, and checkpoint cursor, then uses hysteresis thresholds to checkpoint and lease safe work to the relay/Mac before pendant loss. On reconnect it reconciles leases by idempotency key and emits one compact recovery receipt; it must never silently transfer an irreversible step.
args.why_useful_to_owner: A dying or disconnected pendant would stop being a cliff. The owner would hear only the few things that truly cannot wait, while ordinary research, briefings, and drafts finish elsewhere and are ready when the pendant returns.
args.effort: Medium-high: typed job schema and migrations, relay coordinator, pendant telemetry event, Mac handoff endpoint, reconnect reconciliation, failure-injection tests for power loss and duplicate execution.
args.risk: A stale battery reading could migrate too late or wake the Mac unnecessarily; use hysteresis, timestamps, conservative defaults, and leases. Duplicate work is contained by idempotency keys; unresolved jobs remain visibly pending rather than claiming success. Recovery is cancel/undo where supported plus a receipt explaining the boundary.
args.cost_impact: Small relay storage and polling overhead; occasional Mac wake/network traffic. No meaningful per-request model cost if urgency and thresholds are deterministic.
args.latency_impact: Adds seconds of checkpoint overhead only near a risk threshold; normal interactive requests unchanged. Reconnect recovery should be available within one health poll.
args.security_impact: Authenticated device-to-relay telemetry only; do not replicate private page contents unless the job already authorized it. Preserve per-surface provenance and require owner confirmation at irreversible checkpoints.
depends_on: A durable cross-surface job/checkpoint contract
Pendant battery and link telemetry
Owner-approved urgency and quiet-hours policy
Typed receipts and idempotency already present in the job runner
